full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Jennifer Richards of the University of Cambridge, Katherine Baxter of the University of Northumbria, Kate De Rycker of the University of Newcastle, Andrew Nash of the Institute of English Studies, London and Kathryn Walchester of the University of Liverpool John Moores.

The national subject bodies for English Studies in the UK–English Association, Institute for English Studies, and University English are co-leading a new project which aims to surface the link between academic study and employability by embedding Skills Talk at every educational stage to:

help our students describe and translate what they can do with confidence and agility, and

collect this information so we have a more granular understanding of the skills developed by the study of English Language, Literature and Creative Writing.

Underpinning this project are several premises:

That our students are our best ambassadors.

That knowledge and skills are interconnected, not independent domains.

That there is a need to align a generic approach to skills with a student-led, practical understanding of the disciplinary particularities of skills.

That we must connect ‘locally’ as well as nationally with employers.

Why now?

There is much information in the public domain about the careers that Arts and Humanities graduates enjoy in the arts, business and finance, charity sector, civil service, education, and government (including as prime minister!). So why has the public perception of their prospects not really changed? One reason is that, since 2015, the idea that a STEM degree is the best route to employment has been entrenched in government discourse. Nicky Morgan, Secretary of State, argued in 2015 that

[I]f you wanted to do something different then the arts and humanities were what you chose. Because they were useful for all kinds of jobs. Of course now we know that couldn’t be further from the truth, that the subjects that keep young people’s options open and unlock doors to all sorts of careers are the STEM subjects: science, technology, engineering and maths.

Actually, we know that it is Morgan’s assertion that couldn’t be further from the truth, and that what is needed is not a contest between SHAPE and STEM subjects, but a thoughtful public conversation about the intersection between them. Yet, in 2025, the Post-16 Education and Skills White Paper made no mention of SHAPE subjects in its 72-pages, despite the significant contribution our graduates make to 4 out of the 8 priority sectors that offer ‘the highest growth opportunity for the economy and employers’: the creative industries, digital and technologies, financial services, professional and business services.

We need to take responsibility too. We haven’t always explained what our students can do well. Generic skills are rightly claimed by all subjects. In practice, however, what each one means varies by discipline, although we rarely discuss this. What difference might it make if in English Studies we were able to show how, for example, studying narrative fiction is excellent training for thinking flexibly, one of the Essential Skills identified by Skills Builder with employers: Creativity, using imagination and generating new ideas.

This is not the first HEPI blog arguing for a more granular, disciplinary approach to skills. Kate Daubney’s valuable analysis of curriculum documents ‘surfaced a rich taxonomy of [arts and humanities] transferable skills which are somewhat obscurely embedded’ in them. What is different about this project five years later is that we are foregrounding the student voice, learning from as well as developing how we talk about skills with students.

Finally, we believe that deeply understanding and celebrating the human skills developed by English, and indeed by all other subjects, is exactly what is needed in this age of AI. ‘Anthropic cofounder says studying the Humanities will be “more important than ever”’, reads one newspaper headline, ‘and reveals what the AI company looks for when hiring’. Headlines like these are becoming common. It falls upon us to help our students understand and articulate, as well as develop the aptitudes needed to shape this new world.

Working together is key

Subject bodies are well-placed to co-curate Skills Talk because we are embedded in our communities. We work alongside other arts and humanities bodies via Arts and Humanities Alliance. The English Association works with teachers of English across all sectors, as well as with bodies representing teachers in STEM: the Association for Mathematics in Education and STEM Learning. This matters because embedding Skills Talk offers another benefit: it reveals how much we share in common, as we discovered at our ‘Humanities and STEM’ launch hosted in by CRASSH this year, and shared in our report.

The Skills Talk project aims to capture both the nuance and expansive nature of the skills gained through the study of English, working with varied cohorts of students across the UK HE sector. We hope to illuminate the capaciousness and particularities of our subject, and offer a new way of thinking about skills and their applicability to society more broadly.

full_text:
Fewer international students are studying at US universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released on Monday show.

Overall, US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education (IIE). And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the US,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.

“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the US for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training (OPT) program.

Although the rule hasn’t been finalized, participation in the OPT program dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the US for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.

DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.

Although the US remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 US colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would probably look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.

Politics aren’t the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, the head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a US degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of Nafsa, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

“They’re saying to themselves: ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

Nafsa, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the US economy dropped by $2.4bn this fall.

US colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2m to $4m.

Decades ago, he arrived in the US on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. He eventually went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall’s data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared with a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the US to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice-president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Donald Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight after Trump’s Republican party suffered big losses in the 3 November midterms might halt new policies targeted at international students.

“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.

The post Students want hands-on training in the work of democracy. Colleges are answering appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
KENOSHA, Wis. — Andrew Staff knew the data. The sophomore at the University of Wisconsin-Madison had helped create an information packet for the 26 residents of Kenosha County, each randomly selected and paid $100 to spend a Saturday confronting the local housing crunch. The key question: Could factory-built dwellings help?

But by the end of the six-hour session, during which residents raised and wrestled with one another’s concerns, Staff’s head was spinning. Affordability was just one factor, he noted, ticking off others such as proximity to parks and transportation and the fact that not every resident actually wants their own house.

Days later, Staff switched his major from political science to public policy, newly offered this fall at the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s La Follette School of Public Affairs, which had helped organize the Kenosha event in part to give students real-world experience.

“I don’t just want to think about political theory,” said Staff. “I want to get out there and do things.”

It’s no secret that Gen Z is unhappy with the direction of the country, distrustful of government and concerned about political polarization. But there’s also evidence they want to do something about it: Seventy-nine percent of those polled in April 2026 felt they could make a difference by voting and participating in the democratic process; 38 percent want to run for state or local office, up from 34 percent in 2025. In November’s midterm elections, voter turnout among people ages 18 to 29 was the second-highest in decades, according to one estimate.

Colleges are answering with courses, certificates — and majors — in public policy, which tends to be more hands-on and skills-based than the political science major. Columbia University in July announced a new major in global affairs and public policy, and institutions including the University of Pittsburgh, Kentucky State, the University of Texas at Austin, Georgetown and the University of Virginia have also recently added undergraduate majors in public policy.

Students dig into ho-hum matters like town budgets, but also spicy challenges animating municipal meetings nowadays, like controversies over data centers, use of Flock cameras and — yes — affordable housing.

The focus on experiential learning appeals to today’s students, who tend to be “anxious about whether what they’re studying is going to get them a job,” said Peter Levine, a Tufts University political scientist and philosopher who helped to found the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE). “And public policy seems pretty concrete, like you could work in state government.”

Many young people right now are “very alienated from national politics,” Levine added. That’s “going to turn some of them, I think very wisely, to state and local politics,” which, he noted, “they may have been overlooking.”

Related: Colleges rebrand humanities majors as job-friendly

Many of the newly created majors are expanding fast. Jodi Sandfort, dean of the Evans School of Public Policy & Governance at the University of Washington, whose public service and policy major started last year, said eight students graduated with it last spring — and 118 applied to the major this fall. Sandfort credits the interest to an erosion of teaching about knotty government issues in K-12 schools, and students arriving on campus and “trying to make sense of current events.”

Sandfort said students in the new major recently gathered data, got resident input and made recommendations to ease a controversy over traffic cameras in a local community: “They saw that their work makes a real difference in solving a problem that can create frustration among citizens.”

Susan Webb Yackee, director of the La Follette School at Wisconsin-Madison, said the new major came after enrollment in a public policy certificate program, which started in 2019, rose from 53 to 649 in six years. Students, she said, “are asking for a more applied learning experience.” So far, 42 have enrolled in the new major; university data project it to reach 417 in five years.

The new major requires a course, Advancing Public Policy in a Divided America, that teaches students to learn how to disagree — productively.

On a recent Tuesday in a packed classroom in Ingraham Hall, 29 students in the course were grappling with a question to work that muscle: “What makes a political view ‘reasonable’ or ‘unreasonable’?” It was no softball. Students broke into groups and associate professor Amber Wichowsky set a timer.

When it came time to share, responses were all over the map. One group decided that most everything was reasonable. “If you just reject somebody’s unreasonable view, they’re not going to have any way to change it to where it might become reasonable to you,” one student explained.

Another group wanted facts but worried about trusting their source. Yet another felt people should have the freedom to speak their minds and people should be open to hearing opposing views — but if everyone is viewed equally, how do you draw a line between reasonable and unreasonable?

Wichowsky jumped in: How should people handle views that deny an individual’s right to participate as an equal? “What do we do with prejudice? What do we do with bias? Does that come under the ‘reasonable view’ bucket or not?”

“I’m hoping,” she added, “you’re realizing how darn difficult this is.”

There may be no firm answers, but that’s the point. The promise and the problem of American democracy is that it is slippery, influenced by those who show up and engage. What the new majors and courses intend to offer are skills to join in.

Related: Interested in more news about colleges and universities? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

They’re also designed to make room for teaching students about governance while skirting a third rail in higher education: political ideology. In the aftermath of diversity, equity and inclusion bans, state laws limiting what can be taught in public institutions — not to mention self-censorship by professors and K-12 teachers — the focus on “skills” and teaching students to “speak across the divide” provides nonpartisan appeal.

More college presidents are signing on to this approach: Some 142 have joined a coalition to prepare students to become “civic problem-solvers,” started in 2023 by the Institute for Citizens & Scholars, a nonpartisan nonprofit in Princeton, New Jersey. The group offers faculty training, helps campuses infuse civic training across disciplines and lets campus leaders share approaches and challenges.

This comes as campuses address the criticism that they are ideological bubbles. Tufts, for one, last fall launched the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education to help students “embrace difficult topics and challenging conversations.” Levine sees the new center as offering exposure to students who “may not know what serious conservatives are saying about things, and they should have the opportunity to learn.”

Red state legislatures, of course, have recently funded conservative-leaning “civic centers” like the Chase Center for Civics, Culture and Society at Ohio State University and the School of Civic Life and Leadership at the University of North Carolina as a pushback to a perceived left tilt. They offer courses, and emphasize their role in promoting discourse by, as the Chase Center put it, hosting “spirited, respectful dialogue among participants with varied viewpoints.”

Despite the sheen of civility, this is a contentious moment. An earlier surge of campus interest in participatory democracy arose at a less partisan time in the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s and skewed toward service learning and community work. It “came out of a sense that American democracy needed more participation, more engagement,” said Levine.

That is not the issue now. Rather, the task is to make engagement productive. Convening people with different views for civil dialogue is a first step, but the bigger task is moving from talk to action.

The La Follette Main Street Agenda project — which the Kenosha event was part of — began in 2022 as town halls to address voter concerns. In 2024, it hosted dinners around the state for residents to converse across differences. Now the goal is to seek solutions.

This year and next, Wichowsky, who also has an appointment in the university’s extension school, said she and her students will work with members of the group Leadership Wisconsin and local officials in five locales across the state to lead community assemblies.

The goal, she said, is to have people not just walk up to a microphone and say what upsets them, but to deliberate with others to find an approach everyone can get behind. The housing issue in Kenosha was hardly settled on one Saturday. But the gathering did produce recommendations attendees voted on to share with the Kenosha County Housing Task Force that spanned matters from design preferences to concerns about transportation, zoning, home ownership and energy efficiency.

Related: ‘I can tell you don’t agree with me’: Colleges teach kids how to hear differing opinions

One lesson students are learning is that bite-sized municipal issues are compelling and worth getting their arms around. It’s also the point of a new course, Local Democracy offered for the first time last spring at Olin College of Engineering in Needham, Massachusetts.

The professor, Erhardt Graeff, is also a Needham town meeting member and library trustee who last spring had students attend a meeting where residents debated a classic high-octane issue: Should the town narrow a road and remove parking spaces to make a main street more pedestrian-friendly?

One of the students, Peter Schnell, a senior from Portland, Oregon, majoring in engineering with a focus on sustainability, was stunned when he arrived. “There’s probably 40 or 50 people in the room who are taking their turn saying why they don’t like the plan,” he said. “I was like, ‘Whoa, like these people care.’”

Soon, Schnell, who was working with a nonprofit focused on water and land use, started attending meetings of the Earth Removal Committee in Carver, Massachusetts. The committee oversees permits for excavation, which has become a controversial local issue.

Graeff, who wants students engaging with uncomfortable issues, recently had first-year students in his Democracy and Media class place cards with “a governance scenario” on an axis from “experts deciding versus everyone affected by that issue deciding.” Scenarios included issues like how much lead should be allowed in drinking water, whether to build a new middle school as well as the earlier question of whether to lose a lane of traffic to make a downtown more walkable.

When students shared what produced the most fervent debate, the downtown issue drew sparks; one side argued urban planners should decide city layout while the other said those most affected should decide.

For students, such disagreement that is a regular part of class feels refreshing. “We have very productive conversations here that I haven’t had with adults,” Jada Quijano, from New York City, said afterward.

Maya Dreymann, from Panama City Beach, Florida, said a lot of the conversations they have in class wouldn’t fly in her high school. “Our teacher would be like, ‘OK guys, do not mention this outside of class because then I’ll get fired,’” she said.

Dreymann, however, was clear that tough conversations “need to be had — because we are going to be the next people to have those conversations in the government.”

title: States step up their role picking winners among college majors and training programs

The post States step up their role picking winners among college majors and training programs appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
For years, higher education policy has focused on getting more Americans into college and helping more of them graduate. Now the emphasis has shifted to another question: What are students and the general public getting out of these degrees?

Colleges are being pressed to show that their graduates find good jobs and earn enough to justify the cost of their education. And as criticism of higher education mounts, colleges face additional pressure to show that they are fueling their regional economies.

State policymakers are responding. Both red and blue states are stepping up their efforts to identify which fields are most needed for producing future workers and using those lists to steer subsidies to academic programs — everything from short-term training to graduate school.

A new 50-state report released today by HCM Strategists, a firm that advises on and advocates for higher education policies, documents how states are identifying high-priority fields of study. It’s something of a central planning exercise, trying to predict what will be needed in the future. Some states rely on labor-market data, including wages and projections of occupational growth. Others use human judgment and advice from employers and industry experts. Still others combine the two.

The stakes are high. Roughly half the states incorporate their priority lists into funding formulas, giving colleges additional money for producing degrees in designated fields. Thirty-five states help pay for the costs of starting up a new degree program in high-priority fields.

Nearly every state has a student financial aid program tied to its high-priority fields, too, according to HCM. For example, Virginia has a program that eliminates community college tuition and fees for students who pursue majors it deems in high demand, such as computer science. Some states forgive student loans in desirable fields. Collectively, these incentives can increase the size of some academic departments while leaving others with fewer resources.

All 50 states have some method for designating high-priority fields. Many work backwards. They start by identifying occupations they consider valuable, based on wages or projections of job growth. Then they connect those occupations to college fields of study. If computer programmers are in demand and earn good salaries, for example, computer science programs may be designated as high priority. But that doesn’t mean the state knows whether computer science graduates are actually getting those jobs, or whether those jobs are being filled by people who studied something else.

One obstacle to measuring graduates’ actual outcomes is the limitation of state unemployment insurance records. These databases track workers’ earnings but often don’t identify their precise occupations. A worker in the healthcare industry, for example, could be an accountant, a doctor, a marketer or a cafeteria cook. The state might know that the person works in healthcare and how much they earn, but not what they do.

“When states are trying to set eligibility for financial aid programs, trying to figure out which programs should receive weights in their funding formulas, they are, more often than not, using that proxy alignment, and not looking at students’ actual outcomes,” said Tom Allison, director of state policy and finance at HCM Strategists and one of the report’s authors.

Ten states have upgraded their wage records to include more detailed occupational information. Only seven states use actual employment outcomes for graduates of specific college programs when deciding which fields to prioritize. Three states — Arkansas, Texas and Ohio — go a step further, considering both what students pay for college and what they earn afterward.

Arkansas, for example, compares post-secondary graduates’ cumulative earnings with their educational costs and contrasts that against what high school graduates earn. Then, Arkansas gives a bigger funding boost to programs whose graduates reach a positive return on investment sooner.

Allison says states are improving their data systems, in part to comply with new federal regulations, such as those governing the new federal Pell grants that pay for shorter workforce training programs. Those upgrades ought to improve how states go about identifying high-priority fields throughout higher education.

However, all of these calculations are based on the past. As artificial intelligence, automation and globalization reshape labor markets, states are trying to predict which jobs will be valuable years from now.

Tennessee, for example, is trying to establish itself as a leader in nuclear energy, an industry that doesn’t yet rank highly in the state’s historical employment data. New plants could create thousands of jobs, from welders and electricians to nuclear engineers. Tennessee is among nine states that allow local employers or other members of the public to petition the state to add fields that its data-driven formula might otherwise overlook.

More than half of states, 38, include fields they consider essential to public services or providing “societal value” even if they don’t pay off in the labor market. Connecticut, for example, has designated nursing and social work as priority fields, regardless of what its general methodology might indicate. Oregon has similarly elevated training for teachers of English-language learners to address an acute shortage.

“We see a lot of states trying to balance jobs that may not pay very well, but they know are strategic for the state,” said Allison.

States also face an updating dilemma. If they update their priority lists too frequently, colleges may struggle to plan programs and hire faculty around shifting priorities. But if they wait too long, the lists can become obsolete. Texas, for example, allows a field to fall short of its criteria in two consecutive biennial reviews before removing it from the state’s priority lists.

Government promotion of college academic fields isn’t new. You could go all the way back to the Morrill Acts of 1862 and 1890 that created the land-grant institutions, with the federal government using its resources to promote agricultural and mechanical expertise. But in the last few years, this effort to pick academic winners has gained steam. During the year HCM analysts spent collecting data on state priorities, they had to update it in real time as states passed new policies. Tennessee, for example, updated its methodology for its Workforce Investment Premium this past summer.

As I was reporting this story, I kept thinking about my years in Moscow, where I began my journalism career. In the 1990s, the new Russian government was trying to dismantle central planning and let market forces determine what the economy needed. Now American states, both red and blue, are using public money to steer students and colleges toward the fields they believe their economies will need. It’s not the same kind of central planning, of course. But it is a remarkable flip-flop on who should make these decisions. I’ll be watching to see how it works out.

title: Defending Academic Freedom Requires Confronting Its Limits
summary:
Defending Academic Freedom Requires Confronting Its Limits Sara Brady Mon, 11/16/2026 - 07:43 PM Byline(s) Letters to the Editor Defending Academic Freedom Requires Confronting Its Limits Sara Brady Mon, 11/16/2026 - 07:43 PM
Byline(s)
Letters to the Editor
full_text:
To the Editor:

In his Nov. 2 column, John K. Wilson defends recent political endorsements by the American Association of University Professors and argues more broadly that academic freedom protects professors’ political expression and activism. To make his case, he attacks my recent Washington Times op-ed as hostile to such expression. But Wilson ignores the fundamental challenge my article poses to his sweeping defense of political activism: Can academic associations credibly defend scholarship and academic freedom while supporting political campaigns that undermine both?

The Middle East Studies Association was established to promote the study of the Middle East. Yet in 2021 it declared a “dual commitment to scholarship and advocacy.” The following year it endorsed an academic boycott of Israel, undermining the very scholarly mission it was founded to advance. By its very nature, an academic boycott seeks to restrict scholarly collaboration and exchange, constraining the production and transmission of knowledge about a country central to the field. Yet in the very report Wilson defends, MESA invokes academic freedom to defend political activism aligned with its own anti-Israel agenda. How can an organization that supports restricting scholarship for political ends be trusted to promote and safeguard that scholarship?

AAUP presents an even more troubling contradiction. In 2006, it rightly condemned academic boycotts as inimical to academic freedom. In 2024, with academic BDS supporters occupying key academic freedom leadership positions, it reversed that policy. How can an organization entrusted with protecting academic freedom retain its credibility after abandoning its long-standing opposition to a campaign that restricts the academic freedom and educational opportunities of students and scholars? Wilson addresses neither contradiction. He insists there is no “political activism” exception to academic freedom, but never explains how that freedom could possibly justify activism that suppresses scholarship and restricts the academic freedom of others.

Wilson’s sweeping defense of faculty political activism also has implications for universities themselves. When professors use their academic authority to pressure students into political campaigns, impose political litmus tests or restrict scholarly opportunities for political ends, they subordinate their educational and scholarly responsibilities to politics.

What, then, are the limits of academic freedom when political activism conflicts with professors’ responsibilities to teach and pursue scholarship or infringes on the academic freedom of students and colleagues? Wilson and other defenders of academic freedom have a particular responsibility to answer this question forthrightly. To invoke academic freedom as a sweeping defense of political activism without confronting those limits is to abdicate that responsibility.

title: When Students Are Scattered
summary:
When Students Are Scattered Sara Brady Mon, 11/16/2026 - 03:00 AM Serving rural dual-enrollment students brings up additional challenges. Byline(s) Matt Reed When Students Are Scattered
Sara Brady Mon, 11/16/2026 - 03:00 AM

Serving rural dual-enrollment students brings up additional challenges.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
What’s the best way to offer dual enrollment when schools are physically far apart and each has three or four students who want it?

I’ve been going through policy and practice recommendations, but I haven’t found a good answer to this one. And it’s very much the lived reality on my campus, as well as at many that serve rural areas.

Ten or 15 years ago, there was a strong national movement to replace direct aid to public K–12 schools with vouchers. The groups pushing for it were mostly hoping to redirect the funds, via students, to religious schools. The push largely failed due to an unusual coalition of urban and suburban liberals and rural conservatives. The rural conservatives knew full well that their public schools were hanging on by a thread already, and that thin-slicing the already-small population could destroy them. They understood the concept of critical mass and could foresee what would happen if the population of a given school dropped too far.

We have a similar dilemma with rural dual enrollment.

In the more rural areas we serve, we have high schools physically far apart from each other, often with modest enrollments. They’re commendably eager to offer dual-enrollment opportunities to their students. The catch is that they might have just three or five students who want a given class for college credit, even assuming they have a teacher with the requisite credentials.

We haven’t found an elegant way to handle that.

One way is to co-sit a high school class with a college class. A few students taking, say, an introductory psychology class might be going for college credit, while the rest take it as a high school elective. That works on paper, but it puts the teacher in an awkward position. Either they effectively have two preps for a single class—not great—or they just teach it as a high school class and students who pay at the end get college credit. Not great, either. I’ve even heard of single classes in which some students are taking it as a high school course, some for dual credit and some for AP. That’s a lot to ask of a single teacher and a single prep.

In theory, an online section that sweeps up three students here and two students there could work. But that presumes a willingness to do online classes and the availability of a lab-like space with appropriate supervision in each of the involved high schools. It’s theoretically possible, but a heavy lift. (Some of us also don’t think it’s a particularly great introduction to college.)

In theory, we could insist that either the entire class is taking it for college credit or nobody is. But we charge (some) tuition for the class, so students who want the subject but not college credit would be forced to pay for something they don’t want. If it were taught to the appropriate level of rigor, too, the fail rates might be too high to be culturally acceptable in the school. More likely, it would effectively deny opportunity altogether to the students who actually want it.

I’ve read proposals to help teachers in rural districts get the graduate-level credentials they need to teach college-level material, and I’m all for them. But that doesn’t solve the thin-slicing problem.

title: Can We Agree on How Higher Education Should Change?
summary:
Can We Agree on How Higher Education Should Change? Doug Lederman Mon, 11/16/2026 - 03:00 AM Prescriptions for the industry’s future align more than not. But the overlap would be clearer if groups with ideological differences took fewer potshots at each other. Byline(s) Doug Lederman Can We Agree on How Higher Education Should Change?
Doug Lederman Mon, 11/16/2026 - 03:00 AM

Prescriptions for the industry’s future align more than not. But the overlap would be clearer if groups with ideological differences took fewer potshots at each other.

Byline(s)
Doug Lederman
full_text:
What does higher education need to do differently going forward? Whose opinions matter most? And how much alignment is there—or might there be if we actually started looking for it—among people and groups with different points of view?

I’ve been thinking about this a lot in the wake of this month’s election. But it was on my mind well before that: I wrote last spring suggesting the creation of a bipartisan commission on postsecondary education, less because I thought the world needed another new group than to argue that there’s more agreement about what Americans need from colleges and universities now than our polarized politics (and social media and everything else) might suggest.

I still think this is the case, as I wrote in my last column describing convergence I was seeing: that instead of arguing over the false binary of degrees versus skills-based hiring, many people in higher education and in the business world care first and foremost that people know how to learn.

But a few recent developments reinforce for me that it’s going to take some work to coax everyone out of their comfortable bunkers and get them around the imaginary table, because their worldviews (or at least their political posturing) affect even how they frame the problems we all claim we want to solve.

This occurred to me especially after the release of a report last week by the right-leaning American Enterprise Institute and Johns Hopkins University, “Leading Colleges and Universities in a ‘Back to the States’ Era: Recommendations from a Bipartisan Summit of Leaders and Students.”

I’ll say out of the gate that I welcome the report, both theoretically (I’m generally of the view that the more perspectives there are to draw from, the better) and substantively: The report involved a lot of smart people and gets a lot right, in my opinion. I’ll come back to the good in a bit.

But for a couple reasons, it also shows how far we may be from aligning around a collective vision for higher education’s future.

First, it’s unfortunate that the report’s authors felt they had to work so hard to diminish other perspectives to promote their own. In the report itself and in a Substack post about its release by one of its authors, Joshua Travis Brown, the authors framed their effort as an antidote to what Brown called “long, self-defense studies” by faculty groups at Yale, Cornell and Vanderbilt that are “not what higher education needs right now.”

I have my own problems with the arrogance and self-importance of the so-called elite institutions, and goodness knows the reports produced by those faculties weren’t perfect—I thought Vanderbilt’s was especially cynical and politicized. (Also, last I checked, Johns Hopkins shares a lot in common with those other highly selective, hugely wealthy universities.)

But the fact that the AEI authors felt obliged to dismiss those faculty reports as the wrong approach felt like the kind of dog-whistle call to conservative allies that threatens to undercut the group’s rhetoric of bringing people together “from across sectors and across the political spectrum.” Can’t we all get along? Apparently not so much.

The other issue I’d take with the framing of the AEI and Hopkins report is about the ideological blinders its authors wear in asserting its core premise: that the enrollment and public trust crises facing higher education are being exacerbated by the fact that “Washington is stepping back, guided by a ‘back to the states’ philosophy of federalism that shifts more of the burden of funding and overseeing higher education onto states and institutions.”

The report cites the Trump administration’s shrinking of the U.S. Education Department, freezing of research grants and instituting student loan caps as evidence. There’s a plausible case to be made that the federal government is becoming a less reliable funder of colleges and possibly even of young people after high school, and that it will be less involved in administering higher education programs and operations than it historically has been (which is not very much).

But the idea that the feds are on their way to withdrawing from oversight of colleges and universities is almost laughable in its smaller-government wishful thinking. The last 20-plus years have been marked by a ratcheting up (not down) of federal involvement (if not meddling) by administrations of all political stripes. The Trump administration has done nothing to suggest a change of course, with its proposed “Compact for Academic Excellence” and its pressure on accrediting agencies to take on more oversight, not less.

If AEI wants to argue that the federal government should withdraw more fully from funding, administering and overseeing higher education, that’s a perfectly legitimate contribution to a healthy discourse about the path forward in higher education. (Acknowledgment: I’m one of many participants in another effort, Higher Ed Reimagined, co-led by my friend Zakiya Smith Ellis, that puts at its core the idea that we need a new and different federal role in postsecondary education “that is responsive to the changing needs of today’s students and today’s workforce, without sacrificing the core values that make American higher education great.”) There’s room for both perspectives, but c’mon, AEI, let’s not introduce facts not in evidence.

Now, here’s a bit about what the AEI report gets right, and why it is a useful addition to the numerous other reports in the last year from the Bipartisan Policy Center, the American Association of Colleges and Universities, and the Council on Higher Education as a Strategic Asset.

The report zeroes in on a set of assertions in five major areas that it says colleges and universities must address if they are to respond successfully to the challenging moment they face: competing identities (and priorities), changing demand, institutional sustainability, perceived value, and transformational experiences for students.

I could quibble with some of them, but a lot of the problems it identifies are legitimate:

Many colleges try to be too many things to too many people, often making institutions more alike than differentiated. Most colleges—especially those without billion-dollar endowments or far more applicants than they can enroll—will need to be choosier going forward, ideally starting with the question “Why do we exist?” and then (re-)defining that mission and aligning their programs with it. (My quibble is that the description the report uses for the “typical” dilemma—managing endowments “the size of hedge funds, running professional-style athletics programs, and operating patent offices that compete with Silicon Valley start-ups—much more reflects the “elite” and public flagship universities the report dismisses than the regional publics and privates it purports to be focused on.)

Public trust is declining (along with demand), and colleges and must “adopt flexible, better-targeted models to remain relevant.” I’ve argued much the same, suggesting that colleges focus more on work-based learning for pay or academic credit and offering new credentials to serve working adults.

Given enrollment and financial pressures, many colleges need to purposely shrink and better align their educational and research offerings to serve their regions. “Higher education can no longer afford to be everything to everyone,” Brown quoted one observer as saying. “True fiscal viability comes from replacing unmanaged growth with strategic, mission-aligned research and regional focus.”

Colleges need to define their value not just in terms of postcollege earnings but also civic engagement, long-term health outcomes and social mobility. Again, I’ve written almost exactly the same thing.

Institutions must transform the student experience (in-person and online) to reduce the friction that forces many of them out, and improve their technological infrastructure and policies related to data and artificial intelligence.

Is this exactly my list of the biggest problems facing higher education? No. But the fact that a right-learning think tank widened its circle (and its thinking) to develop a plan that aligns in many ways with those of higher education groups says something about this moment and the potential for a coherent national (if not federal) strategy for improving postsecondary education.

If we stop the sniping.

title: International Student Enrollment Down 9% in Fall 2026
summary:
International Student Enrollment Down 9% in Fall 2026 Johanna Alonso Mon, 11/16/2026 - 03:00 AM Preliminary data from the Institute of International Education found that the number of individuals participating in OPT declined this fall for the first time in five years. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso International Student Enrollment Down 9% in Fall 2026
Johanna Alonso Mon, 11/16/2026 - 03:00 AM

Preliminary data from the Institute of International Education found that the number of individuals participating in OPT declined this fall for the first time in five years.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
International student enrollment in the U.S. continued to decline this year, with the biggest decreases among graduate students at 15 percent, according to new data from the Institute of International Education.

The institute’s fall 2026 snapshot report also shows that new international student enrollment decreased by 15 percent, a slightly less steep drop than the 18 percent decrease in fall 2025. In a major shift from last year, the number of individuals working on optional practical training, a temporary work program for international graduates, declined by 6 percent.

The data, released today, comes from a preliminary survey of about 800 colleges and universities. The organization also released its 2026 Open Doors report, which is a more comprehensive look at international education in the 2025–26 academic year.

Institutions across the U.S. have been struggling with sharp declines in international enrollment since last fall, with institutions that rely on international student tuition revenue especially impacted. This year’s data indicates those declines don’t appear to be easing up.

Overall international enrollment declined by 9 percent, a significantly steeper drop than the 3 percent decrease from fall 2024 to fall 2025, the first fall semester of Trump’s second presidential term. A major part of that drop is OPT; while the number of F-1 visa holders working on OPT in the U.S. continued to increase in 2025 by about 14 percent, they’ve dropped this year for the first time in five years.

The exact cause of the decline is uncertain, though one factor is likely a months-long pause in processing OPT applications for students from countries included in the Trump administration’s travel ban last winter and spring. According to the American Immigration Council’s U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services immigration filing dashboard, the current backlog for postcompletion OPT applications was about four months as of early summer 2026.

The Trump administration is currently attempting to crack down on the program; a recently proposed regulation would require colleges and universities to pay at least $70,000 for each student who applies for OPT.

In the fall snapshot survey, the vast majority of institutions—95 percent—said prospective international students would look elsewhere if OPT was limited. Respondents attributed the overall decline in international enrollment to issues in the visa application process (88 percent), travel restrictions (70 percent), students opting to study in other countries over the U.S. (60 percent) and costs (45 percent).

Undergraduate international enrollment also dipped slightly this fall, by 3 percent; in 2025, undergraduate enrollment stayed about flat.

Taking Stock of 2025–26

The 2025–26 data, which includes data from over 3,000 institutions, mostly confirms what other sources, like the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center’s fall 2025 numbers, have already indicated. International enrollment was down about 3 percent the first fall after President Donald Trump began his second term and quickly implemented a severe deportation campaign, including revoking the SEVIS statuses of thousands of students and detaining several international students who had expressed pro-Palestinian speech. The administration also paused visa interviews for international students for about three weeks, leading to severe backlogs. Colleges had warned those actions would deter international students from coming to this country to study.

The largest losses were among master’s students, which declined by 22 percent. While India still sent the most international students to the U.S. in 2025, the number of Indian students studying here decreased about 6 percent from 2024, and the number of students from the second most popular home country, China, decreased by 4 percent.

But some countries had better luck, with nations like Nepal, Bangladesh, Canada, Italy and Ghana sending record-high numbers of students to the U.S. last year.

International enrollment also decreased across all institution types except community colleges. Enrollment of international students at community college has been increasing for three years, though it has slowed from a 13 percent increase in 2023–24 to a 3 percent increase in 2025–26.

The decline in international students also had different impacts on different states. While some states saw the number of international students at their universities drop sharply, others saw increases. The largest was in New Hampshire, which welcomed 31 percent more international students in 2025 compared to the previous year.

Despite the declines, last year marked the fourth year in a row where there were over a million international students in the country. The U.S. remains the top host country for international students globally.

In an economic study of international students during the 2025–26 academic year, NAFSA: Association of International Educators found that international students contributed $39.9 billion to the economy last year, a 7 percent decrease and a loss of over 46,000 jobs as compared to the previous year. This fall, international student declines are estimated to have cost the U.S. economy $2.4 billion and 31,000 jobs.

“The data again reflect the harsh reality that the barriers the U.S. government is putting in place to block talented international students are having a real impact,” said Fanta Aw, NAFSA executive director and CEO, in a press release.

“We appreciate the 1 million international students currently in this country and applaud the many U.S. colleges and universities that are committed to supporting student success amid challenging circumstances. For our part, NAFSA will continue to use every lever to ensure international students can continue to pursue their educational and career goals here. We stand ready to work with the new Congress and the administration to immediately course correct.”

title: Week in review: Boston, Baylor and Penn State universities in budget holes
summary: We’re rounding up last week’s most interesting stories, from financial woes at major institutions to college campus takeovers in Pennsylvania and Florida.
full_text:
Most-clicked story of the week:

Boston University has so far missed its revenue estimates for the fiscal 2027 year by $42 million, which officials attributed to tuition and enrollment pressures. The news comes after the private institution last year laid off 120 staff members and eliminated another 120 vacant jobs because of budget woes.

Number of the week: 59%

That’s how many U.S. colleges reported drops in international graduate student enrollment this fall, with an average decline of 13%, according to a new survey released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators and others. Meanwhile, 45% of colleges said they had fewer foreign undergraduates enroll. The vast majority said federal policies were creating barriers to international recruitment.

Budget gaps abound:

Boston University wasn’t alone in its fiscal woes. Pennsylvania State University is facing a $124 million budget shortfall. About 70% of that is due to declining tuition revenue, while the rest is from rising employee healthcare costs. To help save money, Penn State plans to limit its president’s strategic funds and modestly reduce nonpersonnel budgets.

Baylor University, in Texas, is navigating a projected $30 million deficit for fiscal 2027 amid sliding undergraduate enrollment and rising costs, among other challenges. To cope, the Baptist institution is freezing hiring and delaying construction projects and capital purchases.

The University of Pittsburgh ended its fiscal 2026 year with a net loss of $644,000, the first deficit it’s experienced since at least 2009, according to The Pitt News, the institution’s student newspaper.The downswing follows declines in grant revenue and increases in employee pay. Officials are reallocating department budgets and offering buyouts to tighten finances.

Colleges expanding with property purchases and acquisitions:

York College of Pennsylvania is taking over Pennsylvania State University’s shuttering York campus. Penn State’s board approved the proposed $7.4 million sale Friday. York plans to turn the campus — a money-loser for Penn State — into a healthcare education center through a partnership with a regional hospital system.

Also on Friday, New College of Florida won approval from the state’s university system board to take out $27.6 million in new debt to support its legislatively mandated takeover of University of South Florida’s Sarasota-Manatee campus. The financing proposal — for $47.5 million total in loans — deviates from system policy in several ways, necessitating approval.

Alvernia University, in Pennsylvania, plans to acquire fellow Catholic institution Marian University, which is hundreds of miles away in Wisconsin. The combination is driven by shared values and plans to combine resources, officials said.

title: Rigorous course participation rose after 2021 law, University of Illinois report finds
summary: The increases in dual credit and Advanced Placement participation in Illinois were particularly notable for Black students and students with disabilities.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Since Illinois passed legislation in 2021 to automatically enroll high school students who exceed state standards in English/language arts, math or science in the “next most rigorous level of advanced coursework,” participation in dual credit and Advanced Placement has increased more than in previous years, according to University of Illinois research.

The policy brief by the university’s Illinois Workforce and Education Research Collaborative shows that a rise in dual credit participation in Chicago Public Schools — the state’s largest district — accounted for the bulk of the statewide increase in 2023-24, the first school year in which the Illinois Education and Workforce Equity Act was implemented. The participation rate increases were particularly notable for Black students and students with disabilities.

Statewide, participation in AP courses accelerated among Latino students and English learners in the 2023-24 school year, according to the study, which also tracked International Baccalaureate courses, honors classes and similar programs. The law was intended to reduce “inequitable access to advanced coursework,” according to the research report.

Dive Insight:

Previous research shows links between success in programs like dual credit and AP, and greater college access and persistence.

Statewide, participation in dual credit courses rose by 17.1% overall in 2023-24 and another 9.1% in 2024-25, as compared with 1.6% and 6.9% in the two previous school years, respectively. Statewide participation in AP courses rose 6.6% in both 2023-24 and 2024-25, as compared with 2.3% the previous year and a participation drop of 5.9% in 2021-22.

While these and other gains were made in the immediate aftermath of the legislation, the study did not attempt to prove a causal relationship, said Sarah Cashdollar, associate director of the Illinois Workforce and Education Research Collaborative.

“Many other things are happening in the state that could be responsible,” she said, including amendments to the state’s Dual Credit Quality Act and higher state appropriations for dual credit and AP courses. “The state, the legislature, and all those who support it are throwing a lot at this issue in trying to improve participation in programs,” she said. “It’s hard for researchers to disentangle the effects of each of them separately.”

Nonetheless, the data describes a positive trend, said Meg Bates, IWERC director. “Certainly, it would have been a disappointment to see it go in the other direction,” she said. We’re excited to see it, and we’ll keep watching it. Hopefully we can do that kind of causal study in the future.”

The IWERC study bolsters other research that shows enrollment in rigorous courses is critical for underrepresented populations, Bates said.

For dual credit, the study found participation rates in 2023-24 increased from the previous year by 28.4% for Latino students and 25.6% for Black students. The year-over-year participation rate increase for Asian students was 15.6% and 13.9% for White students.

For AP, the increases were 9.2% for Latino students, 8.5% for Black students, 4.6% for White students and 3.4% for Asian students.

“Sometimes, we see a general trend that looks one way, but when you go underneath the hood, changes in certain students’ participation” runs counter to the trend, she said. “In this case, we got to see a little bit of both.”

However, she added, “That’s great, seeing more Black and Latino students, and more English learners. But because it’s going up for everyone, some of our gaps are widening.”

Those gaps should spur further research, Bates said, because educators and policymakers don’t want to see student experiences become more asymmetrical. “Following up with districts to understand the ‘why’ is very important.”

Cashdollar would like to see more research into the spikes in participation for English learners and Latino students.

“Was this group previously overlooked despite being capable of taking these classes — so the policy did what it was intended to do, and qualify more students?” she said. “A better understanding of all the different factors at play would be really useful.”

Bates believes a policy like automatic enrollment is uniquely equipped to target English learners. “Educating English learners can be costly for districts and can be hard to staff because you need bilingual educators,” she said.

This is a "nudge" to include English learners in this coursework," Cashdollar said.

title: International student enrollment fell 2.7% in 2025-26
summary: The annual Open Doors report also found signs losses are poised to continue, with the number of new foreign students plummeting 17.7% from the prior year.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

U.S. colleges hosted roughly 1.1 million international students in the 2025-26 academic year, an annual decrease of 2.7%, according to the annual Open Doors report released Monday.

A 22.4% drop in international master’s enrollment, down to 237,655 students, helped drive the overall loss,the report found. Enrollment of foreign undergraduates stayed largely level — dipping just 0.3% to 356,165 — while the number of doctoral students increased3.1% to 158,152.

The report, from the Institute of International Education and the U.S. Department of State, found signs of a weakening international enrollment pipeline that could lead to further losses in the coming years. New international enrollment — foreign students attending their institution for the first time — plummeted 17.7% from 2024-25,marking the second consecutive year of declines.

Alongside the Open Doors report, IIE released a preliminary fall survey of 809 colleges conducted with 10 higher education associations. They found that international enrollment declined 9% at surveyed institutions this fall, driven by a 15% drop in new foreign students and a 15% decrease in international graduate students.

Nearly 9 out of 10 surveyed colleges said the visa process has hurt foreign enrollment, and 70% blamed travel restrictions. Additionally, 60% cited competition from other countries for international students.

“There are more countries actively investing in and recruiting international students,” Mirka Martel, IIE’s head of research, evaluation and learning, said during a press call last week. “As a result, this often means that there are more destination opportunities.”

Just over half of the surveyed colleges that reported growth in new international student enrollment attributed the gains to recruitment efforts and campus athletics programs. Another 44% cited outreach efforts to foreign students who had already applied and been admitted.

Surveyed colleges also reported recruiting international students already within the U.S. Over half, 57%, said they reached out to foreign students studying at U.S. high schools, and 48% sought out international undergraduates for graduate programs.

The countries the U.S. has traditionally relied on for a steady stream of international students — namely, India and China — are sending fewer citizens to study here, according to the broader Open Doors report.

While India retained the top spot, sending 339,435 students in 2025-26, that’s a 6.5% decline from the year prior. China, whose college student population in the U.S. has ticked steadily downward since the pandemic, sent 254,458 students. That’s a 4.3% decrease from 2024-25.

Optional Practical Training participation grows

Despite overall enrollment declines, the Open Doors report found an increase in Optional Practical Training participation. The program allows student visa holders to work in their field of study in the U.S. for up to three years following graduation. In 2025-26, 335,785 foreign students took part in OPT, up 14.1% from the previous year.

Martel said that the growth in OPT over the past four years is due to the post-pandemic rebound in international graduate students. Those students are still making their way through the OPT pipeline, she said.

However, early indicators suggest OPT participation could soon suffer declines as well. IIE’s preliminary fall poll,conducted in October, found that OPT students declined 6% year over year across surveyed colleges.

The drop comes amid news that OPT could get significantly more expensive for colleges.

Early last month, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security proposed up to $100,000 in new fees for each international student a college recommends for OPT.

Many colleges have told the Trump administration they won’t be able to afford the fee. However, the second Trump administration has largely enacted regulations affecting higher ed with few changes from its proposals.

A corroding pipeline of students

The latest Open Doors data reinforces what many colleges and higher ed groups have flagged — that the international student pipeline is constricting.

A new analysis of federal data from the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration found that fewer than 1.1 million international students were studying in the U.S. as of last month, down 6.7% from October 2024.

Miriam Feldblum, the organization’s president and CEO, called the data a warning sign for the U.S.

“The administration’s policies are creating uncertainty at every stage of an international student’s journey,” Feldblum said in a Thursday statement. “While we can’t attribute the decline to any single policy, the cumulative effect makes the United States a less predictable destination and puts our international talent pipeline at risk.”

In a separate survey of some 200 U.S. colleges released last week, nearly 6 out of 10 said they saw fewer international graduate students in fall 2026. The average reported decline was 13%.

Most respondents, 90%, said restrictive federal policies posed a significant obstacle to international enrollment, with some citing the colossal new fees the Trump administration has sought to impose on H-1B visas and the OPT program.

The Common App in August said that first-year international applicants using its platform declined 10% year over year during the 2025-26 cycle.

title: Serbia’s Student List candidates to be sworn in as MPs after election triumph
