full_text:
Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, are to be sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.

The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – will be sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.

A caretaker government under the outgoing prime minister, Ðjuro Macut, will remain in office until MPs approve the Student List’s choice of a cabinet. For now, its makeup – including the identity of a future prime minister – remains unclear.

Sarah El Sarag, a human rights lawyer and MP-elect, said the wider student movement continued to be active in the process of selecting the cabinet, along with the candidates themselves. “We are there because of them,” she said of the students. “All the time, we are doing it together.”

Parliamentary planning sessions had helped prepare the candidates, she said. “We have been having meetings and exercises for the parliament almost every day, because none of us are professional politicians. We are lawyers, doctors, professors – and it is the first time for us to do this kind of job.”

The sessions reflect the Student List’s efforts to pre-empt sceptics who question whether a group of candidates with no political experience is equipped to govern. Members of the movement that selected El Sarag and her fellow MPs-elect have reiterated that all are experts in their professional or academic fields and are better qualified than many of the people who served as ministers or MPs under Vučić.

El Sarag said her colleagues had a good idea of what to expect from Tuesday’s opening session. “People who have had some experience of politics have been making some simulated exercises for us,” she said.

She would not divulge the identity of the candidate for speaker – who will become Serbia’s acting president – let alone the name of the next prime minister.

Vučić is not accepting his new role as leader of the opposition meekly. Since the election, he has accused the Student List of instituting a regime of “naked terror” by directing “submissive prosecutors and police” to carry out unlawful detentions.

Police and prosecutors have made a series of arrests of people with links to the SNS. Last week, prosecutors targeted the owners of a well-connected construction company over a project on the site of the once-famous Hotel Jugoslavija, which was hit during the 1999 Nato airstrikes on Belgrade.

That followed the arrest of the owner of Alta Bank, which held the concession for processing bill payments on behalf of Serbia’s state-owned electricity company. Others facing charges include senior police officers accused of abuse of office, and people suspected of vote rigging and violence during the elections.

After the two years of protests which culminated in the SNS’s defeat at the ballot box, Vučić is threatening major protests of his own.

Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Serbian election and democracy monitor CRTA, said the first disruptions could come during parliament’s inaugural session.

“We can expect a lot of sabotage, a lot of obstruction, a lot of circus-creating atmosphere,” he said. “If we see such scenes in parliament – including some kind of physical obstruction – that’s something which would not surprise me.”

In such an atmosphere, speed may be of the essence, he said. MPs must approve a new cabinet within 90 days of the national assembly’s inaugural session but will be motivated to name a PM well before that deadline.

title: Sir Michael Morpurgo: ‘I was beaten at boarding school for reading after lights out’
summary: The War Horse author says his experiences would be deemed child abuse today and left him with a fierce determination to take fear out of children’s lives
full_text:
Children's author Sir Michael Morpurgo has compared the way he was regularly beaten at school to child abuse.

Sir Michael, author of War Horse, has described how he was reduced to tears by the pain and humiliation of regular canings at his boarding school.

They were often carried out in front of the whole school as punishment for alleged academic failings, even for reading a book under the bed sheets at night.

Recalling his ordeal in a filmed interview with The Independent’s editor-in-chief Geordie Greig, Sir Michael, 83, said his “punishment was harsh and frequent - fear ruled every hour of the day”.

By the standards of today it would be deemed “child abuse”, he said.

The Abbey School in Ashurst Wood Near East Grinstead, where Morpurgo was sent aged seven, closed in 1969.

In a wide-ranging discussion for The Talk Show, Sir Michael also recounted the shock as a teenager on first discovering his real father's identity when his mother pointed him out on television playing Magwitch in a performance of Charles Dickens' Great Expectations.

And committed pro European Sir Michael praised “courageous” prime minister Andy Burnham for saying Brexit could be reversed.

Seventy years after leaving the Abbey School he can remember every detail of his horrifying six years there.

“The abuse... I suffered, was mostly the fear. There was a terrific fear of failure because your marks were read out publicly.

“Every Saturday morning there was an assembly, and all your marks in every subject were read out, how well or how badly you'd done. If you'd done really badly, you walked up the red carpet and you got the cane.”

The young Michael was often among those to be called out.

“Academically, I was never very strong, and this didn't make it any better. I've never forgotten it. I can exactly remember the desk from which he (the headmaster) hid the cane, take it out - he'd hit the back of your thighs when we were in shorts, so it hurt a lot.

“And the tears started in your eyes. You don't forget that sort of thing.

“Sometimes when you get caught doing something you really shouldn't have done, like reading books under the blanket with a torch after lights out, you get more than two strokes, and then it really did hurt.”

Asked if it would be termed child abuse if it occurred today, he replied: “Yes, it would be these days. There is no way schools would do that anymore, they'd be closed down.”

Sir Michael, who was at Abbey Wood from the of age of seven to 13, described it as “a thoroughly unpleasant place”.

“There's no doubt about that. To go away from school when you're seven or eight was strange, and quite lonely, so that you never had a home. You spent more time in the school than you ever did at home.”

There were more tears when he received the one letter per week pupils were allowed to get from their parents.

“Like the beatings, the letters were handed out in front of the rest of the school. I could never bear to read my letter in public because I would always cry. So I would go to the toilet... the only place to be totally alone.

“There were no locks on the doors, so I used to put my foot up against the door and read my letter, and then you cry your eyes out, and no one saw me. And then it was back in front of people again, and I tried not to think about it.”

Sir Michael said his harrowing experiences at school had had a big effect on him as an adult.

It had left him with “a fierce determination... to take fear away from children's lives. Fear of any kind in a school simply should not be there.

“Fear of failure, one of the most corrosive things in a child's life is when you say, ‘I'm no good’.”

A child who left primary school thinking that about themselves could never recover, he said.

His children's books The Butterfly Lion and Who's A Big Billy Then? both reflect his having been the victim of bullying.

Sir Michael's new book, Down Burrow Lane is based on his and beloved wife Clare's decision to buy a farm in Devon half a century ago.

They have since have welcomed more than 100,000 children from towns and cities to experience life in the countryside through their charity, Farms For City Children.

Sir Michael said his own childhood was not helped by his step father who always gave him a “hard time”.

In another interview Sir Michael said his step father once called him “a bear with little brain”.

The marriage of Sir Michael's mother to his birth father ended when he was a toddler. His father Tony van Bridge returned from two years spent overseas on WW2 duty to discover his wife had fallen in love with another man, Jack Morpurgo.

Van Bridge settled in Canada where he became a successful actor and had no contact with the young Michael or his brother.

Sir Michael, aged 19, found out who his real dad was while watching Great Expectations on television at home with his mother and stepfather.

“Suddenly, from up behind a gravestone rears this hideous figure. It's Magwitch. He's a convict. My mother's sitting here, and she went, ‘Oh my God, Michael, that's your father.’

“She had never spoken to me about my father, ever. And there he was as Magwitch on the television.”

Morpurgo's stepfather walked out in a huff.

“And the rest of us sat thinking ‘My God, my father's a convict’. It was quite extraordinary. We knew he was an actor, my brother and I, but that's the first time I met my father.”

Sir Michael praised the way his real father had reacted on returning from the War to learn his wife wanted to marry another man.

He took her on holiday to try to woo her back and when that failed “generously” agreed to let her build a new life with Jack Morpurgo - with Sir Michael and his brother.

“He told her: ‘Look, if we're going to part, I'm not going to hang around and be a part-time father. I know you're gonna marry him and you may have other children, so here's what I'd like to do. When the boys are old enough to decide for themselves, tell them I will always want to see them’.”

Sir Michael duly met Van Bridge shortly after seeing him on TV.

“He came over (from Canada), we sat down and had cups of tea. I remember the tinkling of the spoons on the side of the cup. We didn't know what to say. But he was soon laughing, we were laughing, and he became a good friend.

“It's a very strange thing to have a friend for a father and not just a father for a father.”

Sir Michael is so furious at Britain's exit from the EU he will not bring himself to utter the word ‘Brexit’.

“Leaving the EU was probably the most disastrous thing we've done since the war,” he said.

“The promises made by the people who wanted to leave (were) nonsense, the whole thing. We ended up by losing a huge whack of our trade - just like that.”

Sir Michael said he “took it personally because I am a quarter Belgian. I have children who have married Europeans. All my grandchildren and great-grandchildren are Europeans. I'm not going to be told by any government that I'm not European.”

He is delighted Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to reconsider the issue.

“I'm really pleased because I feel he's understood the mistake that's been made. I think we've got a courageous man as prime minister at last. Someone who does mean what he says.”

title: The new French malaise
summary: The ongoing student protests in France are a symptom of a much larger crisis affecting French society.
full_text:
Fifty years ago, Alain Peyrefitte, who served as a spokesperson for French President Charles de Gaulle, published a book entitled Le Mal français (The French Malaise). In the book, Peyrefitte wrote that the progress of the French nation was impeded by the lack of trust – within society and between society and state institutions. In reaction, the state exercised excessive control through rules, bureaucracy and centralisation, which resulted in stagnation.

Today, the French malaise persists, but its symptoms are quite different from the ones observed by Peyrefitte. We now have the dramatic protests by French students as well as workers and other disaffected groups, which at times have turned violent.

But these demonstrations are only the tip of the iceberg. The malaise runs much deeper.

A threat to the Republic

Following the events of October 17, in which symbols of state authority were attacked – including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille and an official building in Lyon – and businesses were looted, French President Emmanuel Macron stated that these acts sought “to tear down our institutions”.

The use of such strong words reminds one of the rhetoric employed by the French government during the protests of May 1968, when students challenged the established order, and their actions were portrayed as an “attack on the Republic”.

There is, in fact, a tendency to compare the current wave of demonstrations with the events of May 1968. Yet the two movements differ. The protesters of 1968 were calling for more freedom, while today’s protesters are demanding equality and dignity. The former demonstrations were led by privileged youth; the latter are driven by those who have been left behind.

Perhaps a more relevant episode to examine is the upheaval of 2005 in the suburbs of Paris and other major cities following the deaths of two teenagers, Bouna and Zyed, who were pursued by the police.

For three weeks, residents of impoverished neighbourhoods, living on the fringes of society both geographically and socially, expressed their anger at police violence and their own marginalisation.

Two elements of the French malaise were already apparent at the time. First was the deep divide between two segments of society: the prosperous urban population and the marginalised, racialised poor, living in the underdeveloped and underserviced outskirts.

The second was the French police itself, which has overwhelmingly focused on policing the latter with ever-growing brutality.

In any country, a citizen-oriented police force can help build the bonds that unite a nation. But in France, the police is tasked with defending the state, not protecting the citizens.

It does not contribute to the cohesion of a nation. It does not abide by proportionality in the use of force or opt for de-escalation; it openly practises a discriminatory approach to policing which differentiates between affluent neighbourhoods and impoverished areas, between the white majority and the communities of colour.

It is no wonder that upwards of 60 percent of the police and military forces of France vote for the far right.

The French archipelago

In 2019, French political scientist Jérôme Fourquet wrote a book entitled The French Archipelago: The birth of a diverse and divided nation. In it, he argues that France has undergone a societal shift which has fundamentally altered people’s relationship with themselves and with the “other”. As a result, French society has split into small “islands” which are increasingly isolated from one another.

This transformation cannot be attributed solely to immigration. It is, above all, the result of the secession of the elite, which has grown distant and indifferent to the fate of the rest of the nation. This includes the political left, who are now commonly referred to as the gauche caviar (the caviar left).

It has been the elite’s abandonment and self-isolation that has caused the revolt of the masses, rather than the other way around.

The institutions that traditionally fostered socialisation between various groups, bestowing a sense of belonging, including schools, summer camps and compulsory military service, are no longer functioning effectively, or are cancelled.

In this fragmented society, one segment has been picked as a scapegoat for all problems, diverting attention from the real roots of the malaise.

Islamophobia is flourishing in France, as is the belief in the “Great Replacement”, a conspiracy theory that people of colour are meant to “replace” the white majority. Islamophobia has even become institutionalised through legislation and a political culture that has transformed blasphemy into something resembling a duty.

The paradox is that France – compared with its neighbours – has a smaller immigrant population while it espouses a much louder rhetoric about “integration”.

And there is a considerable gap between rhetoric and reality. While those in power demand that people of immigrant background “integrate”, very little is done by the state to actually drive this process.

As a result, some French citizens feel they are French only on paper. They understand that citizenship cannot be reduced to a political discourse. Without genuine access to rights, which necessarily entails social justice and human dignity, there can be no meaningful citizenship.

In 2005, a group of activists went as far as declaring themselves the “Natives of the Republic” and calling for its decolonisation. Indeed, anyone familiar with French society can recognise that France has reproduced a colonial order within.

The country that gave birth to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen has failed to treat some of its own people as full citizens. And that stands at the core of the new French malaise.

title: Jury orders California school district to pay $29m over teacher abuse of pupil
summary: Following allegations of sexual abuse by a teacher at Luther Burbank Elementary School, a former student sought accountability through the legal system. A civil lawsuit against ABC Unified School District led to a $29 million jury award due to negligence, although the district later settled confidentially, obscuring the financial outcome. Additionally, six more lawsuits against the teacher remain active, underscoring serious concerns about how institutions manage abuse allegations.
full_text:
A school is meant to be a place where children are protected, but a former elementary pupil in California has spent years seeking accountability for abuse he says he suffered inside a classroom. His civil case against ABC Unified School District has now resulted in a $29 million jury award, making it the first of seven lawsuits involving allegations against the same former teacher to reach trial. The verdict, announced by the plaintiff's lawyers on November 5, has brought renewed attention to claims that the district knew about the educator's alleged misconduct involving other students but failed to act. Six related cases are still pending. The plaintiff, identified in court-related publicity only as J.O., attended Luther Burbank Elementary School in Artesia, California. According to an announcement issued by his legal team at Herman Law, he alleged that he was sexually abused by a teacher when he was a child. The lawsuit accused ABC Unified School District of failing to protect students despite having prior notice of the teacher's alleged sexual misconduct involving other pupils. The case was tried by Herman Law attorneys Greg Glazer and Justin Felton. The jury awarded J.O. $29 million, according to the firm, which announced the result through a November 5 press release. The lawyers said the case was the first of seven involving allegations against the same former teacher to go before a jury. Six other cases have yet to be tried. The allegations raise questions not only about the conduct of the former educator but also about the responsibility of school authorities when concerns about an employee's behaviour emerge. The plaintiff's central argument was that the district had information about alleged misconduct involving other students and did not take adequate steps to prevent further harm. The claims against the district therefore focused on its alleged failure to respond to warnings and protect children under its care. However, the $29 million figure needs an important qualification. A November 9 report by legal publication Daily Journal said ABC Unified had stipulated to negligence and liability shortly before the trial, leaving the jury to determine damages. The publication also reported that the district said it had reached a confidential settlement with J.O. during the trial and, as a result, would not have to pay the jury's $29 million award. The settlement amount and terms have not been made public. The distinction is significant: the jury's award is not necessarily the amount the plaintiff will receive, and the district's account of the settlement should not be confused with the verdict itself. The publicly available announcement from Herman Law did not disclose the settlement. The district's reported position adds a separate development to the case, while the financial terms remain undisclosed. The six remaining lawsuits could now bring further scrutiny to the district's handling of complaints involving the same former teacher. Each case will have to be considered on its own evidence, including the individual plaintiff's allegations and what school officials knew or should have known at the relevant time. The first trial, however, has placed the broader allegations in the spotlight. The teacher has not been publicly identified in the announcement issued by Herman Law. Nor does the release specify the years during which the alleged abuse took place, the plaintiff's age at the time or the precise circumstances in which the district is said to have received earlier warnings. The case comes amid wider scrutiny of how California school districts have dealt with historical claims of sexual abuse. A December 2025 investigation by the Los Angeles Times found that public school districts across the state had faced more than 1,000 lawsuits since 2020 involving allegations of childhood sexual abuse. The investigation also examined how some districts had resolved claims through confidential settlements, raising questions about transparency and public accountability. The newspaper reported that more than 330 cases had been settled for roughly $700 million at the time of its investigation, while the state projected that local education agencies could ultimately face payouts of between $2 billion and $3 billion as cases moved through the courts. The figures reflect a much wider set of claims across California and are not specific to ABC Unified. For school districts, cases of this nature can involve difficult questions about institutional responsibility: whether complaints were received, how they were investigated, whether employees were allowed to continue working with children and whether appropriate safeguards were put in place. In civil litigation, a district's potential liability can depend on what administrators knew or should reasonably have known and whether their response was adequate.

title: Bengaluru’s Namma Oota Festival: Where food meets science, play and discovery
summary: Returning for its fourth edition on November 21 and 22, Science Gallery Bengaluru’s festival explores how aroma, sight, sound and texture shape our experience of food, with workshops, conversations, food stalls and interactive activities
full_text:
After exploring yearlong exhibitions on topics such as carbon’s role in the culinary arts, food and fermentation, and alternate forms of nutrition, Science Gallery’s latest edition takes a diversion from what we eat to how we experience it. “Our yearlong exhibition seasons work as research festivals. Alongside them, we wanted two smaller festivals that return to each season’s theme in a way that is easy and fun to step into, and where people as well as disciplines meet,” says Jagath V, 32, senior programme associate, spotlighting the upcoming Namma Oota Festival (November 21 and 22).

The Festival, now in its fourth edition, is designed to start meaningful conversations around what is on our plates, in science, stories, people and systems.

“Each earlier edition took its cue from an exhibition-season at the Gallery, from Carbon in 2024 to nutrition in Calorie last December. This year’s festival starts from the senses: how aroma, sight, sound and texture shape the way we experience food,” explains CM Manasvi, 27, programme associate.

Workshops and conversations

The two-day fest will feature a series of events alongside food stalls by women-led collectives, chefs, brands, and science-led food experiences. “The Ragihalli Collective, led by women farmers from Bannerghatta’s ecologically sensitive elephant corridor, serves ragi staples and crisp murukku. Sookta, a women-led collective of 200 members from Sirsi, offers a fizzy twist on the tangy red kokum, and Puli, a South Indian spice and condiments brand, brings heirloom recipes and Coorg-style smashed sandwiches,” says Manasvi, adding that others in the line-up include Oormaakase Kitchen that fuses South Indian food with Japanese omakase; Roar Bakes with unusual pairings; mushroom brand Nuvedo; and their in-house cafe, Ondu Plate @SGB will veer away from South Indian fare to serve burgers and fries.

While the stalls remain at the heart of the festival, the team is taking things up a notch with Aata (Kannada for ‘play’), an activity corner “designed to encourage you to play with food, quite literally!” says Manasvi. “You can sip on lemonade while you paint, get creative with our ‘Write with Your Food’ activity, playfully experiment with the genetics of rice varieties, or tuck into our food library and board games collection.”

Around the stalls and the activity corner, there are a series of workshops, a Namma Ooru food quiz, food karaoke, an open mic, a live music set, a public lecture on coffee and Quantum walkthroughs.

“We have invited home cooks and collectives alongside brands and chefs. We hope to nudge visitors to look at food beyond sustenance and discover the many questions and stories it holds,” says Manasvi.

Highlights include A Cup of Coffee in a Changing World that traces the daily cuppa back to biodiverse forests, smallholder farmers and a changing climate; Open Mic @ Namma Oota that will bring together storytellers, musicians, comedians, poets and singers; and Book an Intergalactic Menu, an astronomical gastronomy workshop pegged on Douglas Adams’ The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy series.

Food at the core

Themes may change at the Gallery, but food continues to be a focal point of all editions. This, courtesy of a growing interest in culinary experiences that the team has witnessed firsthand. “Food has drawn audiences to the Science Gallery since our earliest seasons, and over time it has found its place in the way people engage with our public engagement initiatives,” says Jagath.

In Elements, Edible Elements invited visitors to taste the science of the periodic table, and in Submerge, Sarjapura Curries paired lunch with a session on cooking with edible weeds. Phytopia brought films on indigenous food cultures and Who Feeds Bengaluru?, a two-day programme on how the city eats.

Over time, he says, food moved from a side programme to the centre of their work. “With Carbon, it became a festival of its own, Namma Oota, which has returned with Sci560 and Calorie to this year’s edition,” he says, adding how the latter (which was a year-long exhibition) showed them the appetite around food, science and experiential learning.

“We ran sugar blowing workshops throughout the year to replenish one of the exhibits. Other programmes included Come Eat With Me, a performance that ends in a shared meal, and Yele Oota, a contemporary dance piece built around the banana leaf meal. We also ran an edible insects programme and food walks, including a market walks and food walks. These were well attended, and we keep receiving requests for more,” says Jagath.

Bengaluru’s evolving landscape

Bengaluru’s thriving food culture explains much of this. “Darshinis are always packed, and popular pizza and ramen places open their bookings and sell out within minutes. There is always an appetite for food programming here. It is also a city of organisations working towards a more sustainable food future, and Namma Oota gives many of them a place to meet the public,” he adds.

Since food is already part of people’s lives, it is also an easy way into larger questions, he believes. “A visitor who comes for a meal can leave thinking about farming, climate, health or culture, which is why food has become one of the most interdisciplinary threads in our programming,” concludes Jagath.

title: LPST protests: Keralam mulling lowering teacher-student ratio in govt schools with division fall leading to loss of post
summary: Proposal likely to come up in Wednesday’s Cabinet meet. Implementation is expected to create additional financial burden of ₹50 crore a year
full_text:
In a step towards ending the agitation in front of the Secretariat by All Kerala Lower Primary School Teachers’ (LPST) Rankholders’ Association, the Keralam government is mulling lowering the teacher-student ratio to 1:25 only in government schools where a fall in student strength leads to loss of teaching post.

At present, the teacher-student ratio is 1:30 in lower primary schools. The government is considering reducing this to 1:25 in government lower primary schools where there is a drop in the number of students in order to protect the teachers in that post itself. This in turn will help avoid redeployment of the teachers who are “thrown out” owing to division fall in vacancies arising owing to retirements every year. With this, the retirement vacancies could be filled up from the current LPST rank-lists.

However, the relaxation will not be considered for aided institutions.

Another proposal under consideration is making appointments from LPST rank-lists to vacancies that arise from exempting head teachers from teaching duties in schools that have 150 or more students. At present, the head teacher vacancies (HTV) are filled by appointing teachers on daily wages. This too will result in more appointments from the rank-lists.

Both these proposals are likely to come up in Wednesday’s Cabinet meeting.

Implementation of these two proposals is expected to create an additional financial burden of ₹50 crore a year.

After the LPST rank-holders had intensified their over 130-day protest, saying they would not give up until their demands were met, the Chief Minister’s Office had signalled the intention for further discussions.

Minister for General Education N. Samsudheen had on Monday said the priority was for protest leader S. Valarmathi to regain her health for the talks to be held.

The LPST rank-holders were demanding implementation of the 1:25 ratio across lower primary schools. However, this would incur an additional expenditure of ₹400 crore, the Minister had pointed out.

The latest proposals are expected to assuage the striking rank-holders to an extent and resolve the current impasse.

The government is also pushing for the Kerala Public Service Commission to conduct examinations to various posts on the basis of vacancies reported by the department.

title: Tighter compliance not tactic to manage international student numbers, says UK Home Office
summary:
There is no blanket policy to manage the number of international students coming to the UK through visa refusals or tighter compliance policies, the Home Office has insisted.

The post Tighter compliance not tactic to manage international student numbers, says UK Home Office appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Tighter Basic Compliance Assessment (BCA) thresholds and rising visa refusals are not a covert tactic to keep international student numbers under control, delegates at the international student recruitment conference hosted by Universities UK International (UUKi) heard this morning.

“There is no cap on the number of students that we want to see coming to the UK, but very much a focus on genuine students,” said Oliver Rae, head of work, study, family and Ukraine services at the Home Office.

Instead, he said that changes to the BCA system were in response to an increase in people coming to the UK on a student visa and then claiming asylum rather than engaging with their studies, as well as the fact that the thresholds had not been revised since they were first introduced in 2015.

Rae observed that the Home Office had become more vigilant towards “post-Covid abuse” of the immigration system. Demand for studying in the UK surged to record highs in the years following the pandemic, which at the time was attributed to pent-up demand after years of global lock downs.

“There was significant concern, not just in terms of the swift increase in volume of students at that time, but the associated risks that came with the increase in volume,” said Rae.

The UK government is clamping down on the misuse of the asylum system, with four countries – Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan – currently subject to a total brake on study visa issuance. The government has said it introduced the controversial policy following a noticeable trend in student asylum claims from these nationalities.

Analysis published in The PIE News suggests that other, larger markets offer a similar asylum risk profile but are not yet subject to study visa bans.

While many UK institutions have complained of a surge in visa refusals – particularly for the January 2026 intake – Rae said that the overall refusal rate for the Summer 2026 intake was around 4%.

However, he pointed out that there were some markets that were noticeably higher risk. For example, he said that “we were we were getting close to around a 20% refusal rate of Pakistan in the summer period”.

“Over the last couple of years, we’ve become much more mature to where risk exists, the type of markets and the type of individuals that are targeting the immigration system,” Rae said. “So I think it’s fair to say that, generally speaking, our winter cohort is generally of higher risk than the summer cohort.”

Alex Lock, head of immigration compliance at Anglia Ruskin University, said that markets the institution was recruiting from that had very low visa refusal rates last year had “gone toxic for us very, very quickly”. Snap changes such as these made it important for universities to keep track of and act quickly on real-time data, he said.

Over the last couple of years, we’ve become much more mature to where risk exists, the type of markets and the type of individuals that are targeting the immigration system

Oliver Rae, UK Home Office

“During the summer surge… the only way we knew there was a problem in Nigeria was when we were monitoring our data in real time,” he said.

“What we’re now seeing centrally is universities like ours who have always been under that 4% metric now having a higher refusal percentage and not really knowing what next we can do, having to step in and withdraw from markets,” Lock warned.

Rebecca Sandford, international student policy lead at the Department for Education, stressed that international students remain important to the UK government and she acknowledged that institutions are trying to strike the right balance between compliance and caution “in what is really challenging the landscape at the moment”.

“We know that the BCA changes are significant, and it’s something that we discuss quite regularly with colleagues at UUKi,” she said.

“Our position is that if institutions have better and more timely information about compliance risk, there is greater scope to manage those risks intelligently, rather than simply retreating from particular markets,” she added.

“If we want institutions to recruit internationally with confidence, including across a diverse range of markets and equities, they need to be able to understand how to manage risks effectively.”

UK university stakeholders have also indicated their frustration with what they perceive as an unfair, opaque UKVI interview system that unfairly targets certain students. Sources speaking to The PIE have told stories of students being refused a visa because they did not know minute details of their chosen institution, such as how many trees are on campus or where the nearest bus stop was.

But Rae said that UKVI has interviewed noticeably fewer prospective students this year for the Summer intake. “That’s as a result of being able to gear caseworkers up to looking at risk in more detail and looking at specifics rather than taking a more broad brush approach,” he said.

However, Rae acknowledged that the Home Office could have done more to articulate some of the reasons outside of refusal rates that certain markets are seen as high risk by UKVI. “One of the metrics that isn’t quite clear is some of the data that you provide back to us post student arrivals,” he said, referencing international student completion rates.

However, “there’s an acknowledgement that we we don’t always get the decisions right”, he added.

Lock posited that universities would have a greater chance of quickly responding to perceived compliance risks in certain markets if the Home Office shared this information more transparently. “If that was shared with us, we could join you,” he pointed out.

Sophie Turnbull, director of international student recruitment at UWE Bristol, highlighted the “human impact” of visa refusals on prospective international students, saying this was what “keeps me up at night”.

“It’s no longer [just] these refusals… it’s the stories that sit behind them,” she said.

title: Psychological safety: international higher education needs to make it safe to speak – and safe to listen
summary:
Universities globally have invested heavily in giving students a voice, but creating more opportunities to provide feedback is only part of the equation. Samer Jaffar argues that institutions must consider whether students feel safe enough to speak openly and how that feedback affects those receiving it.

The post Psychological safety: international higher education needs to make it safe to speak – and safe to listen appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Student voice is firmly embedded in how many universities think about the student experience. Surveys, module evaluations, discussion boards and other feedback mechanisms generate extraordinary volumes of insight.

But there is a more fundamental question: Do students feel psychologically safe enough to say what they really think?

For international higher education, that question matters even more, as explored in our new report Wired to Thrive: Student Voice, Belonging, and Institutional Success. Students increasingly study across borders and cultures, entering institutions where expectations around speaking up, challenging authority, and disclosing personal concerns may differ significantly from those at home.

Students may have concerns about wellbeing, how they are treated, diversity and inclusion, harassment or other issues affecting their ability to learn and thrive.

Some will share those concerns through surveys, while others will express them on social media, discussion boards or elsewhere within university systems. Some may not feel comfortable expressing them at all.

Psychological safety therefore needs to become a central part of student voice. It is not enough to provide a mechanism through which students can speak.

Institutions need environments in which students trust that they can raise concerns confidentially, that their identity will be protected where appropriate and, crucially, that somebody will listen.

Listening creates responsibility

There is another side to this conversation which receives less attention. Psychological safety should apply not only to students providing feedback but also to faculty receiving it.

Anyone working with student feedback knows how direct raw comments can be. Valuable criticism can sit alongside personal remarks, identifying information or language that may negatively affect the individual receiving it.

Universities therefore face a balancing act: preserving the authenticity of student voice without unnecessarily exposing faculty to harmful comments or compromising student anonymity.

Explorance MLY can help. Smart redaction can remove identifying or potentially harmful information while preserving the essence of what a student is communicating. It can also help institutions analyse thousands of comments and identify serious issues that might otherwise become buried within large datasets.

If a student raises concerns relating to harassment, substance misuse, suicidal thoughts or another serious matter, that cannot simply become one data point among thousands. It requires attention and potentially intervention.

The real measure of student voice is not how much feedback an institution collects. It is whether people feel able to speak – and whether their university is prepared to act when they do

Students need to learn how to give feedback

Technology, however, cannot solve this alone.

One of the most interesting examples I have encountered comes from a medical school in Saudi Arabia, which we work with at Explorance. As part of onboarding, the institution explains why student voice matters and teaches students how to provide feedback effectively.

The institution presents constructive feedback as part of students’ responsibility and learning journey. The institution achieves response rates above 70%, without incentives or participation blocks.

This is especially relevant for international universities. We talk frequently about creating a culture of listening, but we also need a culture of constructive feedback that works across different nationalities, cultures and expectations.

Students should understand that their voice has value, but also there are people on the other side of their feedback.

From collecting feedback to acting on it

Important lessons are emerging across international higher education.

The UK has developed a particularly strong culture around student voice, which has become a recognised function within many universities, as presented at the recent Explorance Europe Summit 2026 and Student Voices in Higher Education Conference. That experience is attracting interest internationally, including from institutions across Asia and the Middle East seeking to learn from established UK practice.

Elsewhere, governing bodies can be important catalysts. In Australia, for example, sector initiatives are placing greater focus on sensitive issues including sexual harassment in higher education.

When regulators ask institutions not only whether they collect feedback but what they are doing with it, listening becomes an issue of accountability.

For years, higher education has become progressively better at asking students what they think. The next challenge is creating an international education environment in which students feel safe to say what matters, institutions can identify concerns quickly, faculty are protected from unnecessary harm, and students can see evidence that somebody has listened.

The real measure of student voice is not how much feedback an institution collects. It is whether people feel able to speak – and whether their university is prepared to act when they do.

title: US: Total number of international students drops for first time in five years
summary:
While the United States remains the top destination for international students globally, new student enrolments have continued to fall in 2025/26, with a record 18% decline shown by newly released data.

The post US: Total number of international students drops for first time in five years appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
There were almost 50,000 fewer international student enrolments at a US college or university for in 2025/26 compared with 2024/25 – marking an 18% drop – according to The Open Doors 2026 Report on International Educational Exchange, released today.

Conducted by the Institute of International Education (IIE), the report also revealed a 3% decline in total international student numbers in the US. This marks the first time this total has fallen since 2020/21, when the decline was attributed primarily to the impact of Covid-19.

International postgraduate students remained the largest student group in the US, with a total of 423,078. However, this group saw the largest decline in 2025/26, falling by 13%. This was largely driven by a more than 20% fall in master’s student numbers.

While undergraduate enrolments remained fairly consistent, this group still experienced a decrease of 0.3%.

Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning at IIE, said one of the main reasons for these declines is “global competition”.

“There are more countries actively investing in and recruiting international students, so as a result, this often means that there are more destination opportunities. And with rising costs and some of the other factors related to visas…that’s allowing international students to consider their options.”

Despite falling international student numbers, the US continues to hold its position as the world’s top destination for international students.

India, China and South Korea are the top three countries of origin for international students, although numbers from all three declined compared with the previous year.

By investing in global engagement, U.S. colleges and universities enable American and international students to build connections that advance long-term research and economic collaboration. These experiences strengthen U.S. institutions and build relationships that extend beyond students’ time on campus

Jason Czyz, IIE

Following overall growth in international graduate student numbers over the past five years, despite declines in the last two, participation in Optional Practical Training (OPT) increased by 14%. Doctoral student totals also increased by 3%.

Jason Czyz, president and CEO of IIE, said the Open Doors 2026 data underscores the “enduring importance” of international education to the United States.

“By investing in global engagement, US colleges and universities enable American and international students to build connections that advance long-term research and economic collaboration. These experiences strengthen U.S. institutions and build relationships that extend beyond students’ time on campus.”

The impact of the more than 1.1 million international students in the US also contributed nearly $56bn to their economy in 2025 according to the US Department of Commerce.

Alongside the release of the Open Doors 2026 report, IIE also provided a preliminary look at international numbers for the 2026/27 academic year with its Fall 2026 Snapshot on International Student Enrollment.

Collecting responses from 809 US higher education institutions, respondent institutions note a 9% decline in total numbers across all levels in 2026/27, with graduate students dropping the most of all cohorts at 15%.

New student enrolments likewise decreased by 15%.

Institutions reporting declines indicate multiple contributing factors, including the visa application process (88%), travel restrictions (70%), enroling in other countries for higher education (60%), and costs (45%).

The IIE also asked respondents what would happen if there were changes in OPT, of which 95% of institutions said that international students would likely look to another country if OPT was not available.

Despite the decline in international student numbers reported in Open Doors 2026, 81% of US colleges and universities say international student recruitment remains a priority

This snapshot only represents a subset of the nearly 3,000 institutions surveyed by Open Doors, the full picture of 2026/27 enrolment will be analysed in Open Doors 2027.

title: Brazil’s K-12 sector calls for closer collaboration
summary:
International education professionals at the inaugural PIE High Brazil called for stronger collaboration among schools, education agents, independent advisers and government-linked organisations – with students’ interests at the centre of the study-abroad journey.

The post Brazil’s K-12 sector calls for closer collaboration appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Speakers at the inaugural PIE High Brazil discussed how high school students may receive guidance from several professionals as they make decisions about higher education, sometimes with conflicting advice.

The panel stressed that professionals can guide students through applications and help them assess their options, but the final choice belongs to students and their families. “We’re there to guide, to share our knowledge, our experience, to provide our professional opinions,” said Felipe Fonseca, founder and CEO at the consultancy Daqui pra Fora.

But Fonseca pointed out that while education consultants, counselors and agents could break down a students’ options for them, they should not push for a certain outcome.

“One thing that we don’t do is to tell them what to do, because it’s their life, it’s their goal,” he said.

Panelists agreed the solution is open, direct communication – crucially, putting students themselves at the heart of the decision.

One thing that we don’t do is to tell [students] what to do, because it’s their life, it’s their goal

Felipe Fonseca, Daqui pra Fora

“We have a lot of situations where sometimes the dream of going abroad is a dream of the parents, but the students are not really thinking about it, or they’re not really prepared for that,” observed Alexandre Argenta, president of the Brazilian Education and Language Travel Association (BELTA).

Once the student’s own ambitions have been discovered, the options become “vast”, he said.

School-based counselors, who often have close and ongoing contact with students, may refer them to outside specialists when they need additional time or focused support – for example, with writing or refining a college list.

Reggie Aguiar, head of college and career counseling at Escola Concept and the founding president of Brazilian College Counseling Association (BRACCA), described the student as the “pilot”, with advisers and specialists forming the team around them.

The discussion also considered artificial intelligence’s growing role in education advising. Panelists saw potential for AI to speed up research and operations, while emphasising that it cannot replace the human side of interpersonal relationships.

“At the end of the line, there is something called relationship, and this final trust,” said Argenta.

Above all, speakers underscored the importance of honest, student-centered guidance. “The greatest form of respect that we could give is to be honest to them,” Fonseca said, referring to young people navigating decisions about their futures.

Fundamentally, said Simone Ferreira, head of EducationUSA office at PUC-Rio, transparent, open communication with everyone at each stage of the process is key.

“It’s important to have clear communication with the student, with the family, and because they are our clients, and, of course, with our colleagues involved,” she said.

title: Why Massachusetts Has Such a Concentration of Prestigious Colleges

full_text:
Some schools are known for entrepreneurship, others for engineering, music, media, or communication. In Cambridge, research universities are known for work across many fields of study.

A cluster of liberal arts colleges in western Massachusetts is known for its emphasis on undergraduate teaching and learning. These schools make the list because they excel in a particular field or are strong across many areas of study.

Our college prestige index emphasizes schools’ academic reputations. It also considers undergraduate programs and opportunities for research, professional experience, and creative work.

The rankings reflect our editors’ assessment of those qualities. For applicants, the distinctions among these highly selective schools may matter more than their rankings. A school that encourages you to develop a business concept offers a different experience from one that trains you to interpret literature.

21

Clark University Gives Psychology Undergraduates Hands-On Research Experience

Clark University in Worcester 1 offers psychology undergraduates a path to conduct their own investigations into behavior. 2

Look into the questions faculty are asking, the training and time commitment they expect, and how students get started.

At Clark, you can learn what goes into research before you interpret the results.

What exactly do you want to measure, and how do you measure it? If you wanted to learn more about children’s understanding of rules, for example, you’d have to consider whether all kids interpret the directions in the same way. Getting students involved early in the scientific process gives them a better idea of the decisions behind behavioral research findings.

20

Bentley University Teaches Business Through Several Academic Disciplines

For students who want to pursue business, Bentley University in Waltham 1 offers several business majors as well as opportunities to explore related fields. 3

People in the same position may have different responsibilities.

Several departments often have to work together. For example, if a company wanted to explore ways to increase online sales, it might involve people from the technology, accounting, marketing, and inventory departments. To make those decisions, all of these departments need to work together and communicate across their different areas of expertise.

Business majors offer a foundation for a range of business careers, often with room to specialize. People who enjoy working with numbers may do well in analytical jobs. Others might prefer a position that calls for more creative work.

When examining Bentley’s business majors, pay attention to courses that focus on a particular aspect of business as well as those that offer a broader overview. Note whether there are other areas of study that business majors can add and whether any prerequisites require you to start on a certain path early.

That experience may help when Bentley students enter the workforce. They’ll have practiced working with people outside their specialty.

19

Emerson College Builds Degrees Around Communication and the Arts

Communication and the arts are central to Emerson College’s 1 undergraduate programs. 4

Whatever program you’re interested in, the students around you may have similar questions and concerns, even if they work in different media.

For example, if you’re interested in writing, you’ll be thinking about how your choices shape an audience’s response. In media production, you might look at how schedules, recording conditions, and editing shape the final product. In communication, you might start by looking at what your audience already knows.

If communication and the arts are central to what you want to do at school, Emerson is worth checking out. As you compare programs, pay attention to the work students do, including work outside class, and to opportunities for collaboration and portfolio development.

18

Berklee College of Music Trains Students Across Contemporary Music Fields

Berklee College of Music 1 brings together students and faculty working across contemporary music production and performance. 5

For musicians serious about pursuing a career in music, Berklee may be a good fit if they want to see how other musicians and producers approach different parts of the same project.

Taking a few lines of a song and turning them into a finished piece of music might involve choices about instrumentation, arrangement, and recording techniques. One producer’s approach to the song might differ greatly from another’s. An arranger might approach the same song differently again.

Focused training in one of these areas can help musicians hone their craft, and a working knowledge of the other areas can give them a better idea of what to expect from collaborators on future projects.

If you’re interested in Berklee, check audition and degree requirements. Look at whether you’ll be able to take courses outside your chosen concentration.

17

UMass Amherst Offers Honors Courses and a Culminating Thesis

The Commonwealth Honors College at UMass Amherst offers additional coursework and a culminating honors thesis. 7

As a public research university, UMass Amherst participates in the state’s Commonwealth Honors Program. 6

The Honors College may appeal to students who are interested in an honors program and are still deciding what they want to major in. They can explore the range of programs and classes at UMass Amherst. Students can take honors sections, and the required thesis can give them room to explore an interest they wouldn’t otherwise study in class.

For example, a student interested in food production could use the honors project to study the specific conditions that local growers have to deal with. A student interested in history or the creative arts might dedicate more time to a topic than a class would allow.

Check the Honors College admission and completion requirements before applying. It’s worth looking at what the honors program would look like in your intended major.

16

Worcester Polytechnic Institute Requires Projects in Every Major

Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) 1 makes qualifying projects part of its degree programs. 8

WPI’s focus on projects may appeal to students interested in math, science, or engineering who want to apply what they’ve learned in lectures.

The undergraduate catalog describes the different kinds of projects.

WPI’s major projects are extended experiences in which students apply what they’ve learned. Projects can begin with practical problems. Students may need to define success, decide what to measure, determine what stakeholders want, and record what they’ve tried.

Students sometimes come up with solutions they’re confident they can implement, only to discover that their idea of success differs from the client’s. Projects can show students the differences between what they’ve been asked to do in a class and what others consider a job well done.

Look through examples of WPI projects to get a feel for how students form their teams, work with supervisors, and choose project topics.

15

Olin Engineering Students Finish With a Team Design Project

Olin College of Engineering in Needham 1 is small and specializes in design.

Olin’s senior capstone program, in which students complete major engineering projects as members of a team, illustrates the college’s approach. Students work on projects sponsored by organizations outside the college. 9

These sponsors have problems they want solved, and their needs place real-world constraints on what the students can build. For example, a design may have to work with other equipment. Even if the device performs well in a test environment, it may have to be redesigned so it can be manufactured and maintained.

Students can draw on that experience and speak concretely about what they did when they talk to future employers.

Prospective students can examine capstone projects to see what Olin teams do. If you’re interested in working with others to design things, consider how much design you want to do as an undergraduate.

14

Babson College Introduces Entrepreneurship Through a Student Venture

Babson College’s 1 Foundations of Management and Entrepreneurship course is a distinctive part of its undergraduate experience. In this course, first-year students work on a venture with a team of fellow students. 10

In class, students consider what might make their business idea succeed or fail. Choosing a particular business idea as a team means students have to decide what information is relevant and when they should change direction.

For example, their customers may pay for one feature of a product or service and show little interest in a part the team thinks is essential.

They’ll also have to figure out how to delegate tasks and communicate decisions as a team. Applicants should examine what’s expected of students in this class and think about how the experience could shape the rest of their time at Babson.

If you’re interested in learning about starting and running a business, Babson’s approach to undergraduate education could be a good fit for you.

13

Holy Cross Teaches the Liberal Arts in the Jesuit Tradition

The College of the Holy Cross in Worcester 1 centers its undergraduate education on the Jesuit liberal arts tradition. 11

Students interested in policy might ask how studies are conducted and whose voices they leave out. Students interested in science might ask how to explain uncertainty when the public relies on their research. Students in every major can think broadly about questions of ethics, evidence, and responsibility at Holy Cross.

That range of questions may appeal to students who are still deciding on a major. You can browse their majors and common curriculum to see which classes might bring those threads together.

Think about whether that approach to a liberal arts education fits what you want from college.

12

Mount Holyoke Students Can Take Courses at Other Five College Schools

Mount Holyoke College in South Hadley is a member of the Five College Consortium. 12 Mount Holyoke students can cross-register for courses at other member schools. 13

Taking a class elsewhere can help if you’re interested in a course that Mount Holyoke doesn’t offer. Perhaps you’re passionate about politics and would like to take an unconventional political science class or continue studying a language beyond the courses offered on campus.

Before choosing classes at another campus, look at how cross-registration works, how full the classes may be, and how long the trip to and from class will take.

For some students, the appeal is being part of a close-knit community while still having access to courses on other campuses.

11

Brandeis University Supports Undergraduate Research and Creative Work

Brandeis University in Waltham 1 encourages undergraduates to take part in research and creative work. 14

Research at Brandeis can take many forms.

In general, students can pursue a project that interests them, guided by a faculty member. Research at Brandeis gives students the chance to explore subjects in more depth than they might on their own. They can see firsthand how researchers generate knowledge and build on earlier work.

For example, a student interested in culture may notice some inconsistencies in scholarship and realize that there are multiple schools of thought on a subject she previously thought she understood. A student in a lab may learn that getting an experiment to work reliably can be much harder than the published papers on a subject make it seem. These are important lessons about how people produce and use knowledge.

Seeing that process firsthand can help students develop resilience and critical thinking.

Students can get involved in faculty members’ research as volunteers or for course credit. There are also paid research positions for undergraduates.

Looking into the kinds of research projects Brandeis undergraduates work on, along with the awards they’ve won for their work, may give you a better idea of whether the opportunities fit your interests.

10

Smith College Lets Students Shape Their Studies With an Open Curriculum

The open curriculum at Smith College in Northampton 1 gives students a chance to chart their own path. 15 Students at Smith can choose from courses across a wide range of disciplines to pursue particular areas of interest and develop expertise within a chosen major.

They can think carefully about the direction of their college career and use the open curriculum to explore topics of interest from several angles.

A student interested in public space at Smith, for example, might take a class in urban history, learn about principles of design, and then examine how city hall views public space. Each of these classes could provide her with a new lens through which to view public space.

It’s worth using Smith’s advising resources to figure out how early classes fit with later ones and how the open curriculum can help you lay the groundwork for a particular major. As you explore colleges with open curricula, think about the paths you might pursue and when you’d like to make decisions about your major. That can help you figure out whether an open curriculum suits you and whether Smith’s particular approach could help you achieve your academic and professional goals.

9

Northeastern University Gives Work Experience a Place in the Degree Plan

Cooperative education is central to undergraduate studies at Northeastern University. 1 Students in majors ranging from computer science to marine biology can alternate periods of classes and exams with work experience. Northeastern offers undergraduate co-op placements at its Boston campus. 16

For many students, co-op provides a chance to explore a career path before graduating.

Some computer science students, for example, realize that problem-solving skills can matter as much as programming skills. Students interested in lab research might discover that they like following established data-collection procedures. Those experiences can influence which courses students take when they return to class.

On a campus visit, ask how students prepare for co-op, how recruiting works, and whether it’s available in your major. Ask how participation affects housing and degree completion.

Ask for a sample schedule to see how periods of co-op fit alongside periods of classes and the requirements of your major.

8

Boston University Uses the BU Hub to Set General Education Requirements

Boston University’s 1 Hub gives its undergraduate schools and colleges a common framework for general education requirements. 17

Courses in the Hub encourage students to think critically about how people produce knowledge in different disciplines and how ideas circulate in society. For example, students interested in health might take a course that examines how claims about health risks gain credibility in different settings.

Some people apply to college with a career goal in mind. Others are unsure what they want to major in. Both groups can use Boston University’s undergraduate curriculum to balance breadth and focus.

Students can tailor their education by choosing a major or concentration and electives that complement or challenge their field of study. Through BU’s Hub curriculum, students can develop skills in research, reasoning, and communication that they can apply across disciplines.

If you’re applying to BU, look at the undergraduate school or program you’re considering to get a sense of its required courses and how its majors are structured.

7

Boston College Combines Its Jesuit Core With Major Requirements

Boston College’s 1 Jesuit tradition and commitment to liberal arts education shape the core requirements for undergraduates. 18

Accounting and science students may encounter unfamiliar ways of thinking about human behavior. Humanities students may be asked to consider kinds of evidence they seldom see in their own fields.

Boston College’s core requirements give students some common ground on which to build their education. The core helps distinguish Boston College in a state with many highly regarded colleges that have more open-ended requirements for graduation.

Boston College students can develop depth in their majors and learn to think critically and creatively about issues outside their fields. Boston College’s core curriculum encourages students to consider a variety of points of view. The aim is to help them think more critically about issues that matter to them.

The combination of a focused major and a broader core curriculum reflects Boston College’s Jesuit heritage. It’s meant to give students a broad education and room to pursue their own interests.

Prospective students can examine which courses count toward the core. Check how those courses overlap with other requirements and how the core would fit alongside a particular major.

6

Wellesley College Students Can Cross-Register at MIT

Wellesley offers a liberal arts education at a women’s college and several opportunities for academic exchange. 19 One is the chance to take courses at nearby MIT. 20

Cross-registration can give students a way to pursue technical or other interests and take courses that complement the ones available at Wellesley. Students should check eligibility, the preparation required, whether there’s space, and how the course fits their schedule. If you’re considering Wellesley, look for specific MIT courses that would build on what you plan to study.

5

Tufts University Supports Liberal Arts and Engineering in One University

Tufts University’s 1 School of Engineering and School of Arts and Sciences give students ways to explore the same problem from different disciplines. 21

Say, for example, you’re interested in ways to deliver clean drinking water to areas that lack it. Depending on which area of study you pursue, you might delve into the piping infrastructure or the materials science behind getting water from one place to another. You might also examine the effects of unequal access to clean water.

Engineering students can examine the social and cultural contexts in which engineering projects take place. Social science students can look at how communities provide services after crises or disasters.

Your school and department will help determine which classes are available to you. Within those limits, students can explore different aspects of the same problem.

Explore Tufts’ course offerings to get a better sense of what classes are available in your areas of interest. Look into the prerequisites and how much latitude you’ll have to pursue advanced coursework outside your intended major.

Based in Medford and Somerville, Tufts pairs technical and engineering programs with liberal arts programs that examine questions of culture, politics, and society. The mix can suit students who are interested in using several disciplines to solve complex problems.

4

Amherst College Lets Undergraduates Shape Their Course of Study

Amherst College, 1 a residential liberal arts college in western Massachusetts, gives students considerable latitude to design their education through its open curriculum. 22

Students complete first-year and major requirements and choose how their other courses fit together. The college trusts students to make thoughtful decisions about which subjects to explore. Students interested in breadth may find that freedom appealing.

For example, students might decide to read a novel, look at data from the labor market, and learn a foreign language to understand a particular issue from several angles. Figuring out what courses comprise a well-rounded education is, in a sense, part of the education itself.

Amherst also belongs to the Five College Consortium, 12 which gives students opportunities to take courses at nearby schools.

Amherst’s place on our list reflects its focus on undergraduate education and the latitude it gives students to choose their courses.

Applicants to Amherst can look at the college’s advising resources and first-year requirements to see how the college supports students in making these decisions.

3

Williams College Pairs Students for Faculty-Led Tutorials

In a Williams College 1 tutorial, two students and a professor meet to discuss an academic topic. 23 The students take turns presenting their work and critiquing their partner’s.

The format encourages close reading and preparation. Students have to think carefully about the basis for their claims and how they’ll respond to counterarguments.

The small group allows time to revisit material that might be hard to cover in a larger setting. Students can spot gaps in their own reasoning and learn how to offer useful feedback to classmates.

Tutorials are one part of the education at Williams, a small, undergraduate-focused college in Williamstown that emphasizes the liberal arts. Applicants should think about what kind of work they’d want to do in a tutorial.

How would tutorials complement the classes, seminars, research, and internships you might pursue at Williams? Which tutorials are available in the fields you’re interested in? How would the format fit the way you learn?

2

MIT Brings Undergraduates Into Research Through UROP

MIT’s 1 Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program (UROP) helps students find and take part in research projects. 24 Through UROP, undergraduates at MIT can work on open-ended problems.

Early tasks may include setting up experiments, learning to sift through data, or replicating earlier results. Students can gain an appreciation for which methods work in different situations, which may come in handy if they later do their own research.

Some projects may introduce students to new areas of interest by combining disciplines.

Students considering doing research at MIT should look at examples of projects, the preparation they require, and the time they’ll need to set aside.

With its emphasis on hands-on learning and discovery, MIT may appeal to students interested in the sciences, math, or engineering.

1

Harvard College Pairs General Education With University Research Resources

Harvard College draws on the broad range of academic programs and research resources at Harvard University. 1 Its undergraduate education combines those resources with a curriculum that gives students structure and room to pursue their own interests.

The Program in General Education gives students a way to relate their studies to areas outside their concentration. 25 For applicants, that breadth is worth considering alongside how deeply they want to study a particular subject.

Science or engineering students might consider the political, social, or educational implications of new technologies. History or literature majors might explore ways of interpreting data on health care or environmental change.

The best interdisciplinary courses take each field’s methods seriously. Students should research Harvard College’s requirements and concentration options to see how much room they’ll have to pursue their own interests.

The breadth of resources and the structure of undergraduate study together put Harvard at the top of our list.

title: Assobiotec, percorso al 2036 per trasformare la ricerca in industria
summary: Quattro priorità: formazione, trasferimento tecnologico, ricerca e semplificazione. Il ministro Urso: il settore è tra quelli che nella Ue investe di più e genera più valore aggiunto. Greco: «Creare le condizioni affinché le idee possano trasformarsi in prodotti e innovazione»
full_text:
Formazione, ricerca, trasferimento tecnologico e semplificazione. È su questi quattro fronti che Assobiotec-Federchimica guarda all’”Orizzonte Biotech 2036”, un percorso che nasce per trasformare innovazione e ricerca in produzione. Il presidente Fabrizio Greco precisa che non è il piano dell’associazione, ma è «la responsabilità condivisa di un Paese che vuole essere protagonista del proprio futuro». L’associazione ieri ha celebrato quarant’anni di storia al Ministero delle Imprese e del Made in Italy, a Roma, dove ha svolto l’Assemblea pubblica 2026 e ha ribadito le tappe di crescita di un ecosistema in costante espansione e con una forte presenza internazionale. Le previsioni parlano di una tendenza costante e in linea con la rappresentazione degli ultimi dati ufficiali disponibili di Assobiotec-Federchimica, secondo cui nel 2024 il sistema italiano delle biotecnologie comprendeva circa 6.000 imprese, con 53,4 miliardi di euro di fatturato e oltre 102.000 addetti, con una crescita rispettivamente del 5%, del 5% e del 4% rispetto all’anno precedente.

Il biotech italiano si caratterizza per una forte proiezione internazionale. Come rilevato infatti dal recente “Report su interscambio commerciale del settore Life Science” a cura del Ministero delle Imprese e del Made in Italy (MIMIT), con riferimento al solo comparto delle Biotecnologie per la salute, l’export mostra una crescita significativa nel periodo 2021-2025, passando da 8,5 miliardi di euro nel 2021 a 22 miliardi di euro nel 2025. Anche le importazioni registrano un incremento, da 10,1 miliardi di euro a 18,1 miliardi di euro. Il ministro delle Imprese e del Made in Italy, Adolfo Urso, nel suo intervento all’Assemblea, ha ricordato che «all’inizio della legislatura con il ministro della Salute Schillaci abbiamo deciso di insediare qui il tavolo pharma e biotec nella convinzione che sia importante nello sviluppo della nostra politica industriale. Questa assemblea lo dimostra: la vostra è un’industria importante nel Paese, cresce nella Ue più del resto dell’economia, è tra i settori più produttivi e che genera più valore aggiunto e investe sempre più in ricerca e formazione. Il Governo è molto impegnato in sede europea nel sostenere le istanze della nostra industria. Il biotech act, in fase di realizzazione deve servire a facilitare l’attività delle imprese nella ricerca e gli investimenti, oltre a favorire un migliore uso dell’Ai nello sviluppo dei farmaci. È una fase decisiva quella europea in cui il nostro contributo è quello di portare le esigenze del sistema italiano in uno dei comparti di maggiore sviluppo. Nel nostro Libro bianco, il documento di politica industriale Made in Italy 2030, con cui abbiamo voluto portare le esigenze del sistema italiano, il biotech e la salute sono indicati tra quelli che ci stanno dando maggiori soddisfazioni».

Ciò che, però, spesso è mancato è stata una visione di medio-lungo periodo capace di accompagnare l’innovazione lungo l’intera catena del valore, dalla formazione e dalla ricerca allo sviluppo e al trasferimento tecnologico, fino alla produzione e al mercato, in quello che il presidente di Assobiotec, Fabrizio Greco, definisce il Biotech Journey. Dalla salute, in una prospettiva One Health, alla sicurezza alimentare, fino alla transizione ecologica, il biotech rappresenta oggi una leva fondamentale per affrontare le grandi sfide del presente e rafforzare la competitività del Paese. Greco evidenzia che «in uno scenario internazionale in cui Stati Uniti e Cina corrono e l’Europa accelera con i lavori sul Biotech Act, anche l’Italia deve saper stare al passo. Dobbiamo creare le condizioni affinché le idee possano trasformarsi rapidamente in innovazione, prodotti e valore per la società, lavorando in maniera sinergica e coordinata lungo tutte le tappe del Biotech Journey: il percorso che porta un’idea a diventare un prodotto innovativo. Per farlo servono una visione di lungo periodo, regole certe e la capacità di fare squadra».

Il primo passo del progetto, presentato nel corso dell’Assemblea pubblica, è il documento «Le crepe del sistema – Il quadro, le sfide e le prospettive». Il percorso di «Orizzonte Biotech 2036» proseguirà in dicembre con la pubblicazione del nuovo rapporto realizzato da Assobiotec in collaborazione con il Politecnico di Milano. Nel 2027 entrerà quindi nel vivo il confronto con gli stakeholder dell’intera filiera biotech nazionale. Nel corso dell’assemblea è stato consegnato l’Assobiotec Award 2026 a Diana Bracco, Presidente e Amministratore Delegato dell’omonimo Gruppo, per la «straordinaria vocazione imprenditoriale» e la capacità di valorizzare la ricerca scientifica e promuovere l’innovazione tecnologica, contribuendo alla crescita e alla competitività del sistema industriale nazionale. Il riconoscimento rende omaggio anche al suo ruolo nella nascita e nello sviluppo di Assobiotec: Diana Bracco ha infatti creduto fin dagli inizi nel valore strategico delle biotecnologie e nell’importanza di dar loro una rappresentanza.

Tema centrale, a maggior ragione alla luce dell’accordo su rappresentanza, contratti e salari raggiunto la scorsa settimana tra sindacati e rappresentanza datoriale.

«Intesa importantissima - osserva il presidente di Assolombarda Alvise Biffi - che pone le basi per successivi accordi specifici e che testimonia come le parti sociali, anche su questioni complesse, sono capaci di trovare un terreno comune e assumersi responsabilità condivise».

Il confronto ha preso le mosse dalla ricerca, realizzata da Assolombarda in collaborazione con Adapt. Tra 2005 e 2015 la quota di imprese aderenti a un’associazione datoriale è scesa dal 64% al 44%. Le imprese che restano associate, però, sono mediamente più grandi, più produttive, più orientate all’export, all’innovazione e alla formazione: si tratta di una rappresentanza più selettiva. Allo stesso tempo, la contrattazione nazionale copre la quasi totalità dei rapporti di lavoro - il contratto applicato è individuabile in circa il 99% dei casi - con livelli tra i più alti d’Europa, pur in assenza di un’efficacia erga omnes stabilita per legge. Le regole prodotte dalle parti sociali raggiungono così una platea ben più ampia di quella che contribuisce a costruirle e a sostenerle. A fine 2024 risultavano depositati al Cnel 1.017 contratti collettivi nazionali, contro i 267 del 1995. Ma 722 di questi si applicano a meno di mille dipendenti, mentre il 97% dei lavoratori è coperto da contratti sottoscritti dalle organizzazioni comparativamente più rappresentative. Il problema, dunque, non è il numero dei contratti, ma i casi in cui perimetri concorrenti insistono sulle stesse attività e la scelta del contratto è guidata dalla ricerca del costo più basso: è il terreno del dumping contrattuale. Per questo, misurare la rappresentatività, anche delle organizzazioni datoriali, è oggi una priorità.

Secondo lo studio, la disintermediazione non ha eliminato il bisogno di mediazione: ne ha cambiato le condizioni. Più il quadro normativo, contrattuale e produttivo si frammenta, più crescono i costi che la singola impresa - soprattutto se piccola - deve sostenere per orientarsi, e più torna centrale chi è in grado di ridurli. La legittimazione delle associazioni non è più garantita dalla sola presenza ai tavoli: va dimostrata con la capacità di produrre conoscenza, coordinare e generare utilità collettiva.
